docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
Every script and module entry point in the repository, with what it does, a usage example and its help text. Run the commands from the repository root: the scripts open config.yaml and camera_calibration.json by relative path.

Command Purpose python decision_testbench.py Evaluate the decision pipeline on the conformance scenarios. python run_experiments.py Run every experiment in the paper in sequence. python run_height_pitch_sweep.py Monte Carlo sweep over camera height and pitch. python crosswalk_analysis.py Performance against road width for one and two cameras. python generate_figures.py Write the publication figures. python sim_visualizer.py Render schematic scenario videos. python -m bikeped.scenarios List, inspect, validate, evaluate, generate and export scenarios. python -m bikeped.sim Probe a CARLA server, start one, and render scenarios. python calibration/calibrate_fisheye.py Fit the lens model to checkerboard frames. python calibration/capture_calibration.py Capture checkerboard frames from a live camera. python calibration/compare_fisheye_models.py Fit four projection models and compare their error. python tools/eval_models.py Evaluate detector checkpoints and cache per-class AP and AR. python tools/latency_report.py Per-step latency statistics from a recorded run. python tools/carla_find_crosswalks.py Extract crosswalk geometry from a CARLA map. python tools/build_docs.py Build this site. python bridge.py Run the live starter-kit bridge (from bridge_starter/).

docs.title: decision_testbench.py
docs.text:
Runs the scripted scenarios through the decision pipeline and prints one row of frame counts and rates per scenario. The mode flags are checked in this order, and the first one present decides what runs: --error-map, --compare, --monte-carlo, --latency-sweep, --optimize. With no mode flag, the default configuration runs once over all scenarios.

python decision_testbench.py --compare                    # every named configuration, with localisation error
python decision_testbench.py --no-bbox-noise --compare    # the same without localisation error
python decision_testbench.py --monte-carlo --mc-trials 50 --failure-model gilbert --burst-length 3
python decision_testbench.py --optimize --w-fn 5 --w-fp 1 --w-lat 2

--no-bbox-noise applies to the five modes. The plain run without a mode flag never adds localisation error, which is why its totals equal those of --no-bbox-noise --compare for the default configuration. --failure-model and --burst-length are read by --monte-carlo only, and the three --w-* weights by --optimize only.

usage: decision_testbench.py [-h] [--optimize] [--error-map] [--compare]
                             [--monte-carlo] [--mc-trials MC_TRIALS]
                             [--failure-model {iid,gilbert}]
                             [--burst-length BURST_LENGTH] [--bbox-noise]
                             [--no-bbox-noise] [--w-fn W_FN] [--w-fp W_FP]
                             [--w-lat W_LAT] [--latency-sweep]
                             [--eval-cache EVAL_CACHE]
                             [--eval-model EVAL_MODEL]

Decision Testbench

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  --optimize            Optimize decision parameters
  --error-map           Print BBox error analysis
  --compare             Compare pipeline configurations
  --monte-carlo         Run Monte Carlo with stochastic detection failures
  --mc-trials MC_TRIALS
                        Number of Monte Carlo trials (default: 50)
  --failure-model {iid,gilbert}
                        Detection failure model: iid (default) or gilbert
  --burst-length BURST_LENGTH
                        Mean burst length for Gilbert model (default: 3.0
                        frames)
  --bbox-noise          Include fisheye BBox localization error (default: on)
  --no-bbox-noise       Disable fisheye BBox localization error
  --w-fn W_FN           Severity-weighted FN weight (default: 5.0)
  --w-fp W_FP           False positive weight (default: 1.0)
  --w-lat W_LAT         Latency weight (default: 2.0)
  --latency-sweep       Sweep camera latency 0–500 ms and generate figure
  --eval-cache EVAL_CACHE
                        Path to eval_cache.json from eval_models.py
  --eval-model EVAL_MODEL
                        Model name in eval cache to use (default: first)

docs.title: run_experiments.py
docs.text:
Calls the testbench once per experiment, then generate_figures.py and sim_visualizer.py --no-display, and stops at the first step that fails. The script's docstring puts the full run at about 45 minutes and the run with --skip-optimizer at about 10.

python run_experiments.py --skip-optimizer

usage: run_experiments.py [-h] [--skip-optimizer]

Reproduce all paper experiments

options:
  -h, --help        show this help message and exit
  --skip-optimizer  Skip the optimizer (saves ~30 min)

docs.title: run_height_pitch_sweep.py
docs.text:
Takes no flags. It sweeps 13 camera heights (1.5 to 7.5 m) against 10 pitches (0 to -90 degrees) on a 40 ft road with 20 Monte Carlo trials per cell, and writes height_pitch_sweep.json to the current directory. If eval_cache.json is present, its measured recall replaces the flat defaults.

python run_height_pitch_sweep.py

docs.title: crosswalk_analysis.py
docs.text:
Takes no flags. It evaluates the pipeline as a function of road width for one-camera and two-camera deployments and prints the result.

python crosswalk_analysis.py

docs.title: generate_figures.py
docs.text:
Takes no flags. It writes six figures as EPS and PDF into paper/: fig_height_pitch, fig_ar_curve, fig_deployment, fig_pipeline, fig_combined and fig_warning_budget. The height-pitch heatmap needs height_pitch_sweep.json and the recall curve needs eval_cache.json; each is skipped with a message when its input is missing. The script does not create the output directory:

mkdir -p paper
python generate_figures.py

Three scripts do not parse arguments

run_height_pitch_sweep.py, crosswalk_analysis.py and generate_figures.py ignore their command line. Passing --help starts the run.

docs.title: sim_visualizer.py
docs.text:

Done.

docs.title: calibration/calibrate_fisheye.py
docs.text:
Fits the equidistant lens model to checkerboard observations by bundle adjustment and writes camera_calibration.json. One of --images or --video is required.

python calibration/calibrate_fisheye.py --images calibration_frames/*.jpg --fit-distortion

usage: calibrate_fisheye.py [-h]
                            (--images IMAGES [IMAGES ...] | --video VIDEO)
                            [--interactive] [--board-width BOARD_WIDTH]
                            [--board-height BOARD_HEIGHT]
                            [--square-size SQUARE_SIZE] [--pad-size PAD_SIZE]
                            [--crop-size CROP_SIZE] [--interval INTERVAL]
                            [--max-frames MAX_FRAMES]
                            [--initial-fov INITIAL_FOV] [--fit-distortion]
                            [--output OUTPUT] [--visualize]
                            [--save-viz SAVE_VIZ]

Calibrate equidistant fisheye camera

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  --images IMAGES [IMAGES ...]
                        Image paths or glob patterns showing checkerboard
  --video VIDEO         Video file containing checkerboard frames
  --interactive         Interactively select frames from video (requires
                        --video)
  --board-width BOARD_WIDTH
                        Inner corners along board width (default: 9)
  --board-height BOARD_HEIGHT
                        Inner corners along board height (default: 6)
  --square-size SQUARE_SIZE
                        Checkerboard square size in metres (default: 0.025)
  --pad-size PAD_SIZE   Preprocessing pad size (default: 3840)
  --crop-size CROP_SIZE
                        Preprocessing crop size (default: 3500)
  --interval INTERVAL   Frame sampling interval for video mode (default: 30)
  --max-frames MAX_FRAMES
                        Max frames to use from video (default: 50)
  --initial-fov INITIAL_FOV
                        Initial FOV guess in degrees (default: 200)
  --fit-distortion      Also fit k1, k2 radial correction terms
  --output OUTPUT       Output JSON file consumed by mqtt_bridge /
                        decision_testbench / sim_visualizer (default:
                        camera_calibration.json). A sibling .yaml with the
                        full bundle (preprocessing block, config_yaml_updates)
                        is written next to it.
  --visualize           Show reprojection visualizations per frame
  --save-viz SAVE_VIZ   Directory to save reprojection images

Fisheye Camera Calibration
==========================

Calibrates the equidistant fisheye model (r = f * theta) used by mqtt_bridge.py.
Standard OpenCV fisheye calibration uses Kannala-Brandt with polynomial distortion
coefficients, which does not fit this 200-degree spherical lens on a 16:9 sensor.

This script uses a custom bundle adjustment that directly fits the equidistant
projection model to checkerboard observations.

Parameters calibrated:
    cx, cy         : optical center in the preprocessed frame (pixels)
    focal_length   : equidistant projection focal length (pixels)
    k1, k2         : optional radial correction terms (r = f*(theta + k1*theta^3 + k2*theta^5))

Usage:
    # From a set of images showing a checkerboard:
    python calibrate_fisheye.py --images calibration_frames/*.jpg

    # From a video (extracts frames at an interval):
    python calibrate_fisheye.py --video calibration.avi --interval 30

    # With a known board size and square dimensions:
    python calibrate_fisheye.py --images *.jpg --board-width 9 --board-height 6 --square-size 0.025

    # Enable radial correction terms for higher accuracy:
    python calibrate_fisheye.py --images *.jpg --fit-distortion

    # Interactive mode: step through a video and press 's' to select frames:
    python calibrate_fisheye.py --video calibration.avi --interactive

Compare fisheye projection models

options:

                        Image paths or glob patterns

Compare fisheye projection models
=================================

Runs calibration with each supported projection model on the same
checkerboard frames and reports RMS reprojection error for each.

docs.title: Configuration reference
docs.text: Two files hold the parameters of a site: config.yaml for runtime settings and camera_calibration.json for the calibrated lens. This page lists every key of both, its shipped value, and which code reads it.

docs.title: Who reads what
docs.text:
Reader From config.yaml From camera_calibration.json decision_testbench.py camera.height, camera.pitch_deg fov_deg, radius_px, frame_width, frame_height, pad_size, cx, cy, k1, k2 sim_visualizer.py --errors camera.height, camera.pitch_deg fov_deg, radius_px, frame_width, frame_height, pad_size, cx, cy generate_figures.py loads the file through load_camera_calibration() calibration/calibrate_fisheye.py writes the file bikeped/sim/fisheye.py (CARLA fisheye view) camera.fov, camera.radius, camera.cx, camera.cy, camera.k1, camera.k2, camera.pitch_deg fov_deg, radius_px, cx, cy, k1, k2, which override the config.yaml values

No other code in this repository opens config.yaml. The remaining keys configure the live bridge of the reference deployment (mqtt_bridge.py), which is not included here. The starter kit does not read config.yaml either. It holds the same settings as constants in its USER CONFIG block, and the tables below name the matching constant where there is one.

Two consequences are worth knowing before you edit the file:

  • Changing the decision block does not change testbench results. The testbench takes its parameters from DecisionParams and PIPELINE_CONFIGS in decision_testbench.py, whose default entry carries the same values as the shipped decision block.
  • If config.yaml is missing, the testbench uses a camera height of 3.048 m and a pitch of 0. If camera_calibration.json is missing, it prints No camera_calibration.json found, using defaults and uses the defaults of FisheyeCamera.

docs.title: video
docs.text: Key Default Unit Meaning use_webcam true Read the live camera instead of a file. Kit: USE_WEBCAM. file_path "06022025_19.avi" Video file used when use_webcam is false. Kit: VIDEO_FILE. process_every_k_frames 1 frames Frame subsampling factor of the live bridge. The kit processes every frame.

docs.title: preprocessing
docs.text: Key Default Unit Meaning pad_size 3840 px The frame is centred on a black square of this side. Kit: INPUT_PAD_SIZE. crop_size 3500 px Side of the centre crop taken from the padded square. All intrinsics refer to this cropped frame. Kit: INPUT_CROP_SIZE.

docs.title: camera
docs.text:
Key Default Unit Meaning height 3.6576 m Mounting height above the ground (12 ft). Read by the testbench. Kit: CAMERA_HEIGHT_M. fov 197.90 deg Field of view across the image circle. Kit: CAMERA_FOV_DEG. radius 1750 px Radius of the image circle. Kit: CAMERA_RADIUS_PX. pitch_deg 0 deg Tilt of the optical axis. Negative looks down. Read by the testbench. Kit: CAMERA_PITCH_DEG. cx, cy 1752.69, 1804.54 px Optical centre in the cropped frame. Kit: CAMERA_CX, CAMERA_CY. projection "linear" Projection model, see projection names. Kit: CAMERA_PROJECTION. k1, k2 0.0, 0.0 Radial terms of r = f (θ + k1 θ³ + k2 θ⁵), used with linear only. Set them from a calibration run with --fit-distortion. Kit: CAMERA_K1, CAMERA_K2. latency_frames 0 frames Frames of measured camera latency to compensate by first-order kinematic prediction. 0 disables it. At 30 FPS one frame is 33 ms, so the value is the measured latency in milliseconds divided by 33.

The intrinsics appear twice, here and in camera_calibration.json. The testbench reads them from the JSON file. After a calibration run, calibrate_fisheye.py prints the camera.fov and camera.radius values to copy into this block, and camera.cx and camera.cy when the optical centre is more than 5 px from the frame centre.

docs.title: detection
docs.text: Key Default Unit Meaning model_path "yolo11x.engine" Detector weights or TensorRT engine. The kit downloads yolo11xxl.pt instead, see YOLO_HF_FILE. confidence 0.1 Detection confidence threshold. Kit: YOLO_CONF. input_size 1280 px Inference size. Kit: YOLO_IMGSZ. valid_classes [0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 31, 36, 37, 16] COCO class IDs kept. The code in this repository names 0 person, 1 bicycle, 2 car, 3 motorcycle, 5 bus, 7 truck, 9 traffic light and 16 dog. Kit: YOLO_CLASSES, which keeps the first six. tracker "bytetrack.yaml" Tracker configuration of the live bridge. The kit tracks on the ground plane with its own GroundPlaneTracker.

docs.title: decision
docs.text:
Key Default Unit Meaning bike_memory_frames 58 frames Stage 2 stays open while a cyclist was seen within this many frames. Kit: DEC_BIKE_MEMORY_FRAMES. prox_min 1.9 m Lower bound on the bike to pedestrian distance that can alert. Kit: DEC_PROX_MIN_M. prox_max 24.8 m Upper bound on that distance. Kit: DEC_PROX_MAX_M. prox_speed_min 0.147 m Minimum cyclist displacement over the lookback for an alert. Kit: DEC_PROX_SPEED_MIN. lookback_frames 2 frames Lookback k of the closing check. Kit: DEC_LOOKBACK_FRAMES. max_range 25 m Agents farther than this from the camera are skipped in stage 3. Kit: DEC_MAX_RANGE_M. max_object_age 10 frames Listed in the file and in DecisionParams. DecisionPipeline has no such argument and no code in this repository reads the key. speed_adaptive true Extend the upper bound to the cyclist's stopping distance when that is larger. Kit: DEC_SPEED_ADAPTIVE. cyclist_reaction_s 0.84 s Perception-reaction time in the stopping distance. Kit: DEC_REACTION_S. cyclist_decel_ms2 1.96 m/s² Deceleration in the stopping distance. Kit: DEC_DECEL_MS2.

The two braking values are the 85th-percentile field measurements of Martin and Bigazzi (2025) cited in decision_pipeline.py. The decision pipeline describes how each parameter enters the three stages.

The constructor defaults of DecisionPipeline are a different set (bike_memory_frames=77, prox_min=0.5, prox_max=20.7, prox_speed_min=0.098, lookback_frames=1). The testbench and the kit pass every parameter explicitly, so those defaults only apply if you construct the class yourself without arguments.

docs.title: tracking
docs.text: Key Default Unit Meaning history_frames 5 frames Read by the live bridge only. The file gives no description. min_track_points 4 points Read by the live bridge only. The file gives no description. speed_window 4 samples Read by the live bridge only. DecisionPipeline estimates cyclist speed over a fixed window of 4 samples.

docs.title: feedback
docs.text: Key Default Unit Meaning blinking true Read by the live bridge only. The file gives no description. go_signal true Read by the live bridge only. The file gives no description. sound_threshold 60 Read by the live bridge only. The kit throttles sounds with SOUND_THROTTLE_FRAMES.

docs.title: mqtt
docs.text: Key Default Unit Meaning enabled true Publish track messages. Kit: MQTT_ENABLED. broker "test.mosquitto.org" Broker host name. Kit: MQTT_BROKER. port 1883 Broker port. Kit: MQTT_PORT. topic "bikeped/intersection/tracks" Topic. Kit: MQTT_TOPIC. username, password null, null Credentials. Kit: MQTT_USERNAME, MQTT_PASSWORD. client_id "bikeped_tracker" Client identifier. Kit: MQTT_CLIENT_ID. qos 0 Quality of service. Kit: MQTT_QOS. publish_interval 1 Read by the live bridge only. The kit publishes every frame.

docs.title: latency
docs.text: Key Default Unit Meaning enabled false Collect per-frame latency data. Kit: LATENCY_ENABLED, which defaults to True. save_path "latency_data.npy" Output array. Kit: LATENCY_SAVE_PATH. save_interval_frames 500 frames Checkpoint period. Kit: LATENCY_SAVE_INTERVAL. warmup_frames 30 frames Frames discarded at start while the model warms up. Kit: LATENCY_WARMUP_FRAMES.

docs.title: Top level
docs.text: Key Default Unit Meaning debug false Debug switch of the live bridge. Kit: DEBUG. verbose false Verbose logging. Kit: VERBOSE.

docs.title: camera_calibration.json
docs.text:
Written by calibrate_fisheye.py. The shipped file is the calibration of the reference camera.

camera_calibration.json
{
  "model": "equidistant",
  "cx": 1752.69,
  "cy": 1804.54,
  "focal_length": 1013.31,
  "fov_deg": 197.9,
  "radius_px": 1750.0,
  "k1": 0.0,
  "k2": 0.0,
  "rms_error_px": 4.6334,
  "num_frames": 42,
  "num_points": 1470,
  "frame_width": 3500,
  "frame_height": 3500,
  "pad_size": 3840,
  "crop_size": 3500
}
Key Shipped value Unit Meaning model "equidistant" Projection model that was fitted. calibrate_fisheye.py always writes equidistant. cx, cy 1752.69, 1804.54 px Optical centre in the cropped frame. focal_length 1013.31 px/rad Equidistant focal length f in r = f θ. fov_deg 197.9 deg Field of view derived from the focal length: 2 · radius_px · 180 / (f · π). radius_px 1750.0 px Half the side of the cropped frame. k1, k2 0.0, 0.0 Radial correction terms. Zero unless the run used --fit-distortion. rms_error_px 4.6334 px RMS reprojection error of the fit. num_frames 42 frames Checkerboard frames used. num_points 1470 corners Corner observations used. frame_width, frame_height 3500, 3500 px Size of the cropped frame the intrinsics refer to. pad_size, crop_size 3840, 3500 px Preprocessing the calibration frames went through.

FisheyeCamera in the testbench does not read focal_length. It computes the focal length from fov_deg and radius_px, which gives the same 1013.3 px for the shipped file. The quality fields (rms_error_px, num_frames, num_points) and model are a record of the calibration run and are not used at runtime here.

The calibration script also writes a sibling camera_calibration.yaml with three blocks: calibration (the values above without the frame and preprocessing sizes), preprocessing (pad_size, crop_size) and config_yaml_updates (the camera.fov and camera.radius values for config.yaml).

docs.title: Projection names
docs.text:
camera.projection and the kit's CAMERA_PROJECTION use the names in the first column. The calibration tools use the model names in the second.

Config name Model Formula linear equidistant r = f · θ equalarea equisolid r = 2f · sin(θ / 2) stereographic stereographic r = 2f · tan(θ / 2) orthographic orthographic r = f · sin(θ)

θ is the angle between the incoming ray and the optical axis, and r is the distance from the optical centre in pixels. calibrate_fisheye.py fits the equidistant model only. compare_fisheye_models.py fits all four on the same frames so you can check which one your lens follows.

docs.title: File formats
docs.text: This page documents the data files the repo reads and writes: scenarios and suites, the scenario catalog, the output of a CARLA render, and the files produced by the calibration, evaluation and latency tools.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
A scenario is a Python dict, or the equivalent JSON object. The testbench reads four keys and ignores the rest.

{
    'name': 'Fast Approach',
    'expected_dominant': 'alert',
    'vehicle': 'ebike',
    'agents': [
        {'type': 'person', 'id': 1,
         'path': [{'x': 5, 'y': -4, 't': 0}, {'x': 5, 'y': 4, 't': 6}]},
        {'type': 'bike', 'id': 2,
         'path': [{'x': 25, 'y': 0.5, 't': 2}, {'x': 1, 'y': -0.1, 't': 4}]},
    ],
}
Key Type Required Meaning name string yes Unique display name. expected_dominant idle, safe, warning, alert yes Expected dominant state: the most severe state (alert > warning > safe > idle) that the pipeline holds for at least 0.3 s in total over the run. vehicle bicycle, ebike, aashto no Braking profile. Defaults to bicycle. agents list yes Pedestrians and cyclists. agents[].type person, bike yes Agent class seen by the decision pipeline. agents[].id integer yes Track id, unique within the scenario. agents[].path list yes Waypoints in time order. agents[].path[].x metres yes Position along the road. agents[].path[].y metres yes Position across the road. agents[].path[].t seconds yes Time of the waypoint. Positions between waypoints are linear in time.

The crosswalk centre is at (5, 0). The frame is drawn in Scenarios and the path rules are listed in Authoring.

docs.title: Metadata keys
docs.text:
bikeped.scenarios, the CARLA renderer and the docs read these. The testbench ignores them.

Key Type Meaning id string Slug, unique across all suites. suite string Suite name. family string Family key. description string One or two plain sentences. tags list of strings Free-form labels. render object Optional rendering hints, such as {'weather': 'wet_night'}. agents[].model string Optional appearance hint for the renderer. agents[].label string Optional short label.

docs.title: Suite file
docs.text: A suite file is a JSON file written by python -m bikeped.scenarios generate --out suite.json. The scenarios inside it use the format above. See Generators.

docs.title: Scenario catalog
docs.text: The catalog is the machine-readable index of every registered scenario. python -m bikeped.scenarios export --out docs_src/assets/scenarios writes it as catalog.json, next to one SVG thumbnail per scenario named <id>.svg. The catalog tables in Conformance suite and Extended suites are written by tools/build_docs.py from the registry itself and use the same thumbnails.

docs.title: Render output
docs.text:
One run of python -m bikeped.sim render writes one directory. Its name is <engine>_<scenario-id>_<weather>.

renders/<run_id>/
  manifest.json                 run metadata, per-frame records, camera models
  video/<view>.mp4              clean view, H.264
  video/<view>_overlay.mp4      view with the HUD
  video/composite.mp4           chosen layout
  frames/<view>/000000.jpg      only with --save-frames
  gt/<view>.jsonl               one line per frame
  stills/                       first frame, first alert frame, closest approach

The directory is described from the user's side in CARLA output.

docs.title: manifest.json
docs.text:
The manifest holds the run metadata, the camera model of every view and one record per frame. The exporter in bikeped/sim/export.py reads these top-level keys:

Key Meaning run_id Name of the run. Falls back to the directory name when absent. run Run metadata, described below. views Names of the rendered views. cameras Camera model per view name. videos Relative path of the clean video per view name. The default is video/<view>.mp4. gt Relative path of the ground-truth file per view name. The default is gt/<view>.jsonl. frames_dir, frame_ext Relative directory of the saved frames per view name and their file extension, present when frames were saved.

Run metadata (RunInfo in bikeped/sim/types.py):

Field Type Meaning scenario_name, scenario_id, suite string Which scenario was rendered. fps integer Simulation and video frame rate. Default 30. duration_s float Scenario duration in seconds. engine ue4, ue5 Unreal generation of the CARLA server. server_version, client_version string CARLA versions reported at connect time. map string CARLA map name. crosswalk_id integer or null Entry of crosswalks.json the scenario was placed on. weather, quality, drive, ambient string Presets and modes the run used. seed integer Random seed. views list of strings Names of the rendered views. site object Site geometry derived from the crosswalk. pipeline_config string Key of PIPELINE_CONFIGS used for the decision states. extra object Anything else the runner recorded.

Frame record (FrameRecord.to_dict):

Field Type Meaning index integer Frame number. The first frame is 0. t float Scenario time in seconds, rounded to four decimals. state string Decision state of the frame: idle, safe, warning or alert. states object Decision state per named pipeline configuration. alert_pair [bike_id, ped_id] or null The pair that triggered the alert. danger object or null Ground-truth danger assessment of the frame. agents list One agent record per agent present in the frame.

Images and auxiliary depth or instance buffers are not written to the manifest.

Agent record (AgentState):

Field Type Meaning id integer Agent id from the scenario. kind person, bike Agent class. sx, sy metres Scripted position in the scenario frame. The decision pipeline and the danger model work on these values. heading radians Scripted heading in the scenario frame. speed m/s Scripted speed. location [x, y, z] metres Centre of the actor's 3D box in the CARLA world frame. rotation [pitch, yaw, roll] degrees Orientation in the CARLA world frame. extent [forward, right, up] metres Half sizes of the box. role scripted, ambient Whether the agent comes from the scenario or from ambient traffic. model string Appearance hint from the scenario. blueprint string CARLA blueprint that was spawned. track_error_m metres Ground-plane distance between the scripted and the simulated position.

Camera model (CameraModel):

Field Type Meaning name string View name. kind pinhole, fisheye Projection. width, height pixels Image size. position [x, y, z] metres Camera position in the world frame. forward, right, up unit vectors Camera basis in the world frame. Image u grows with right, image v grows against up. fov_deg degrees Horizontal field of view for a pinhole view, full field of view of the image circle for a fisheye view. cx, cy pixels or null Principal point. Null means the image centre. f_px_per_rad pixels per radian Fisheye focal length. k1, k2 number Fisheye polynomial terms: r = f (θ + k1 θ³ + k2 θ⁵). circle_radius_px pixels Radius of the fisheye image circle.

docs.title: gt/<view>.jsonl
docs.text:
The file has one JSON object per line and one line per frame. Line k belongs to frame k of the clean video of the same view.

Field Meaning index Frame number, the same as in the manifest. t Scenario time in seconds. width, height Image size in pixels that the boxes refer to. When absent, the size of the view's camera model applies. objects One entry per agent, with the fields below. Object field Meaning id, kind, role As in the agent record. bbox Axis-aligned 2D box [x1, y1, x2, y2] in pixels, origin at the top-left corner. corners_image The eight projected corners of the 3D box. distance_m Distance from the camera in metres. truncation Fraction of the box that falls outside the image. visible_fraction Fraction of the agent that is not occluded, available when depth or instance buffers were rendered.

To turn one view into a detection dataset, run python -m bikeped.sim export RUN_DIR --format coco|yolo. The exported classes are person and bicycle; a scenario agent of type bike becomes bicycle. See Ground truth.

docs.title: Tool output files
docs.text:
File Written by Read by Contents camera_calibration.json calibration/calibrate_fisheye.py testbench, visualizer, renderer Calibrated fisheye intrinsics. Every key is listed in Configuration. eval_cache.json tools/eval_models.py decision_testbench.py --eval-cache One entry per model name. Under merged, the classes pedestrian, cyclist and vehicle each carry ap5095 and recall, and optionally per_size and ar_curve. latency_data.npy the bridge, when latency profiling is on tools/latency_report.py A 2D array with one row per processed frame and ten columns: frame_acquire, preprocess, yolo_preprocess, yolo_inference, yolo_postprocess, bev_tracking, decision, viz_submit, total, pipeline_only.

How the detector statistics enter the testbench is covered in Uncertainty models, and the latency columns in Latency.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text: A scenario is a scripted encounter between pedestrians and cyclists at one crosswalk, written as timed waypoints. This page covers what a scenario contains, the coordinate frame, the suites that ship with the repo, and how to reach them from Python and from the command line.

docs.title: Scenario dict
docs.text:
A scenario is a plain Python dict: a name, the state the warning light should show for most of the run, an optional braking profile, and a list of agents that each follow a path. This is Fast Approach from the paper's conformance set, as it appears in decision_testbench.SCENARIOS:

{
    'name': 'Fast Approach',
    'expected_dominant': 'alert',
    'vehicle': 'ebike',
    'agents': [
        {'type': 'person', 'id': 1,
         'path': [{'x': 5, 'y': -4, 't': 0}, {'x': 5, 'y': -2, 't': 1.5},
                  {'x': 5, 'y': 0, 't': 3}, {'x': 5, 'y': 2, 't': 4.5},
                  {'x': 5, 'y': 4, 't': 6}]},
        {'type': 'bike', 'id': 2,
         'path': [{'x': 25, 'y': 0.5, 't': 2}, {'x': 13, 'y': 0.2, 't': 3},
                  {'x': 1, 'y': -0.1, 't': 4}]},
    ],
}

The pedestrian walks across the road in six seconds. The cyclist appears at t = 2 and covers 24 m in two seconds. The testbench steps the scenario at 30 FPS, interpolates every agent at each frame, feeds the positions to the decision pipeline and labels the frame with the ground-truth danger model. The field-by-field reference is in Authoring and File formats.

docs.title: Coordinate frame
docs.text:
Scenario coordinate frame seen from above: x along the road, y across it, crosswalk centred at (5, 0), camera at (5, -13) 0 10 15 20 25 30 35 -10 -5 5 10 x (m) along the road y (m) across the road cyclist path x: 34, y: 2, t: 0 pedestrian path x: 5, y: -6, t: 0 crosswalk centre (5, 0) crosswalk max_range: 25 m from the camera camera (5, -13) The scenario frame seen from above, with one illustrative cyclist path and one pedestrian path.

Coordinates are metres on the ground plane and times are seconds. The table lists the two axes and the two fixed points of the frame.

Axis or point Meaning x Along the road. Cyclists travel along it. y Across the road. Pedestrians cross along it. (5, 0) Centre of the crosswalk. The visualizer and the browser simulator draw its stripes from y = -12 to y = 12. (5, -13) Default camera position (FisheyeCamera.cam_x, cam_y). The camera looks along +y, across the road. t Seconds from the start of the scenario.

Headings are derived, not authored: interpolate_agent returns the direction of the current path segment in radians, with 0 pointing along +x.

The pipeline receives positions relative to the camera, as it does on the deployed system. max_range (25 m in config.yaml) is therefore a distance from the camera at (5, -13), and an agent on the road at x = 34 is outside it until it gets closer.

docs.title: Suites
docs.text:
A suite is an ordered list of scenarios with a name. list_suites() returns the names that are registered.

The conformance suite is the paper's set of 24, kept in decision_testbench.SCENARIOS and never edited, because every number in the paper comes from it. See Conformance suite. Two more suites are registered next to it:

Suite Scenarios Contents conformance 24 The paper's scenarios, unchanged, in paper order extended 41 Hand-designed urban conflicts and deliberate negatives in twelve families stress 8 Dense scenes with 12 to 24 agents for throughput and tracker load

Both are described in Extended suites. Generators produce further suites on demand from six parametric families.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
from bikeped.scenarios import list_suites, get_suite, get_scenario, all_scenarios

list_suites()                        # suite names
conformance = get_suite('conformance')   # the paper's 24, in paper order

get_scenario('fast-approach')        # by id (slug)
get_scenario('Fast Approach')        # by exact name
get_scenario('conformance:7')        # by suite and index

every = all_scenarios()              # all suites, concatenated

Each returned dict is a normal scenario with extra metadata keys (id, suite, family, description, tags). The testbench ignores those keys, so a registry scenario can go straight into simulate_scenario:

from decision_testbench import PIPELINE_CONFIGS, FisheyeCamera, simulate_scenario
from bikeped.scenarios import get_scenario

result = simulate_scenario(get_scenario('fast-approach'),
                           PIPELINE_CONFIGS['default'], cam=FisheyeCamera())

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
Command What it does python -m bikeped.scenarios list Lists scenarios. --suite and --family filter, --json prints machine-readable output. python -m bikeped.scenarios show ID Prints one scenario: metadata, agents and waypoints. python -m bikeped.scenarios validate Checks every scenario for structural errors. --suite limits the check. python -m bikeped.scenarios evaluate Runs scenarios through the decision pipeline and reports the metrics. Takes --suite, --config and --json. python -m bikeped.scenarios generate Samples a new suite from a family and writes it to a JSON file. See Generators. python -m bikeped.scenarios export Writes catalog.json and one SVG thumbnail per scenario. 
usage: python -m bikeped.scenarios [-h] COMMAND ...

List, check, evaluate, generate and export bike-pedestrian scenarios. Suites:
conformance, extended, stress.

positional arguments:
  COMMAND
    list      list scenarios with suite, family, agents and duration
    show      print one scenario as JSON
    validate  check format, speeds and unique ids; exit 1 on problems
    evaluate  run the decision pipeline with ideal perception and summarise
    generate  write a seeded parametric suite as JSON
    export    write catalog.json and one SVG thumbnail per scenario

options:
  -h, --help  show this help message and exit

docs.title: Authoring scenarios
docs.text: This page shows how to write a scenario by hand, what each field means, how paths are interpolated, and how to check the result and run it through the testbench.

docs.title: A complete scenario
docs.text:
A pedestrian crosses while a cyclist approaches, slows down and stops short of the crosswalk.

late_braker.py
scenario = {
    'name': 'Late Braker',            # unique display name
    'expected_dominant': 'alert',     # most severe state held for >= 0.3 s
    'vehicle': 'bicycle',             # braking profile (optional)

    # Metadata: used by bikeped.scenarios, ignored by the testbench.
    'id': 'late-braker',
    'suite': 'local',
    'family': 'standard',
    'description': 'A cyclist brakes late and stops two metres from the crosswalk.',
    'tags': ['braking'],

    'agents': [
        # Pedestrian: 12 m across the road in 8 s, so 1.5 m/s.
        {'type': 'person', 'id': 1,
         'path': [{'x': 5, 'y': -6, 't': 0}, {'x': 5, 'y': 6, 't': 8}]},

        # Cyclist: 6 m/s for 3 s, slows over the next 3 s, then waits at x = 7.
        {'type': 'bike', 'id': 2,
         'path': [{'x': 33, 'y': 0.5, 't': 0}, {'x': 15, 'y': 0.5, 't': 3},
                  {'x': 7, 'y': 0.5, 't': 6}, {'x': 7, 'y': 0.5, 't': 8}]},
    ],
}

Coordinates are metres in the scenario frame, with x along the road, y across it and the crosswalk centre at (5, 0), and times are seconds.

docs.title: Scenario fields
docs.text:
Key Required Values Meaning name yes string Display name, unique across suites. Results are reported under it. expected_dominant yes idle, safe, warning, alert The dominant state the run should produce: the most severe state (alert > warning > safe > idle) that the pipeline holds for at least 0.3 s in total over the run. vehicle no bicycle, ebike, aashto Braking profile for ground-truth labelling and for the pipeline's stopping distance. Defaults to bicycle; an unknown value also falls back to bicycle. agents yes list One entry per pedestrian or cyclist.

Each entry of agents has three required keys. The optional appearance keys are listed under Metadata.

Key Values Meaning type person, bike Which side of the pipeline the agent feeds. Anything that rides counts as bike. id integer Unique within the scenario. The pipeline uses it as the track id. path list of {'x', 'y', 't'} Waypoints in time order.

docs.title: Path rules
docs.text:
The testbench reads paths through two functions in decision_testbench.py. interpolate_agent gives an agent's position and heading at a time t, and get_scenario_duration decides when the run ends. Their behaviour comes down to the following points.

  • Position is linear between consecutive waypoints. Speed is constant on a segment and changes at the waypoint, so a smooth acceleration takes several short segments.
  • An agent exists only between its first and its last waypoint time, both included. Outside that interval it is absent from the frame, as if it had not been detected. Start a path late to make an agent enter mid-scenario; the cyclist in Fast Approach starts at t = 2.
  • Waypoint times must increase. Two waypoints with the same t make a segment of zero duration, and interpolation divides by that duration.
  • To hold an agent still, repeat its position with a later time, as the cyclist above does between t = 6 and t = 8.
  • Heading is the direction of the current segment, in radians, 0 along +x. A stationary segment reports 0.
  • The scenario runs until the latest last-waypoint time plus 0.5 s. Late Braker runs for 8.5 s, which is 256 frames at 30 FPS.
  • Keep the encounter within max_range of the camera (25 m from (5, -13) by default). Stage 3 of the pipeline skips agents beyond it.

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
The scenario library, the renderer and these docs read a few extra keys. The testbench ignores them.

Key Meaning id Slug, unique across all suites. Used on the command line and in file names. suite Name of the suite the scenario belongs to. family Family key used for grouping and filtering. description One or two plain sentences. tags List of free-form labels. render Optional rendering hints, for example {'weather': 'wet_night'}.

Agents accept two optional keys: model, a rendering hint for the CARLA renderer (adult, child, wheelchair, runner, bicycle, road_bike, ebike, escooter, cargo_bike, moped), and label, a short text shown next to the agent.

docs.title: Validate
docs.text:
python -m bikeped.scenarios validate

The command checks every registered scenario and exits with a non-zero status if one fails.

docs.title: Run it through the testbench
docs.text:
simulate_scenario takes the dict directly. Append this to late_braker.py and run it from the repository root:

late_braker.py (continued)
from collections import Counter

from decision_testbench import (
    PIPELINE_CONFIGS, FisheyeCamera, get_scenario_duration, simulate_scenario,
)

result = simulate_scenario(scenario, PIPELINE_CONFIGS['default'], cam=FisheyeCamera())

print('duration', get_scenario_duration(scenario), 's,', len(result['times']), 'frames')
print('states  ', dict(Counter(result['states'].tolist())))
print('TP/FP/FN/TN', result['true_pos'], result['false_pos'],
      result['false_neg'], result['true_neg'])
print(f"sensitivity {result['sensitivity']:.1%}  specificity {result['specificity']:.1%}")
print(f"alert latency {result['alert_latency_s']:.2f} s  "
      f"min warning budget {result['min_warning_budget_s']:.1f} s")

$ python late_braker.py
duration 8.5 s, 256 frames
states   {'warning': 110, 'alert': 146}
TP/FP/FN/TN 85 61 0 110
sensitivity 100.0%  specificity 64.3%
alert latency 0.00 s  min warning budget 4.8 s

The pipeline is in alert for 146 of the 256 frames. Of those, 85 are actionable danger frames and none are missed. The other 61 fall on frames that the danger model labels safe, which is where the 64.3% specificity comes from. The metrics are defined in Conformance suite.

cam=FisheyeCamera() places the camera at its default position (5, -13), so the pipeline sees camera-relative positions as it does in python decision_testbench.py. Without cam, positions are passed in scenario coordinates and max_range is measured from the origin. To add the fisheye localisation error, pass add_bbox_noise=True together with the camera; the error model is described in Perception.

docs.title: Conformance suite
docs.text:
The conformance suite is the set of 24 scripted scenarios behind every result in the paper. This page lists them, explains how a run is scored, and shows what the default pipeline does on each one.

The scenarios live in decision_testbench.SCENARIOS and are not edited. bikeped.scenarios exposes the same list, in the same order, as the suite conformance.

docs.title: The 24 scenarios
docs.text:
The table is read from decision_testbench.SCENARIOS. Duration is the last waypoint time plus 0.5 s (get_scenario_duration), rounded to 0.1 s.

# Scenario Expected state Pedestrians Cyclists Duration (s) Braking profile 0 Safe Crossing safe 1 0 6.5 bicycle 1 Bike Approaches Ped alert 1 1 7.5 bicycle 2 High-Speed Near Miss alert 1 1 6.5 bicycle 3 Multiple VRUs alert 3 2 8.5 bicycle 4 Occluded Emergence alert 1 1 6.5 bicycle 5 Parallel Paths warning 1 1 8.5 bicycle 6 Bikes Only idle 0 2 5.5 bicycle 7 Fast Approach alert 1 1 6.5 ebike 8 Speed Variant alert 1 2 10.5 bicycle 9 Counter-Flow on Crosswalk alert 1 1 6.5 bicycle 10 Multi-Speed Converging alert 2 3 8.5 bicycle 11 Wheelchair User alert 1 1 27.2 bicycle 12 Stopped Pedestrian alert 1 1 13.5 bicycle 13 Cross-Street Cyclist alert 1 1 8.5 bicycle 14 E-Scooter alert 1 1 7.5 ebike 15 Child Pedestrian alert 1 1 13.8 bicycle 16 Overtake from Behind alert 1 1 12.5 bicycle 17 Cyclist Abort safe 1 1 8.0 bicycle 18 Dense Pedestrian Group alert 8 1 10.4 bicycle 19 Diagonal Jaywalker alert 1 1 9.5 bicycle 20 Swerving Cyclist alert 1 1 8.0 bicycle 21 Late Turn Toward Ped alert 1 1 7.5 bicycle 22 U-Turn Cyclist alert 1 1 8.5 bicycle 23 Accelerating E-Bike alert 1 1 7.5 ebike

Twenty scenarios expect alert, two expect safe, one expects warning and one expects idle.

Twenty-one of the 24 contain at least one frame that the ground-truth danger model labels as dangerous. The three that contain none are Safe Crossing, Parallel Paths and Bikes Only. In two scenarios, Occluded Emergence and Fast Approach, every danger frame is too late for a warning to help the pedestrian, so they have danger frames and no actionable ones (see Scoring).

docs.title: Families
docs.text:
bikeped.scenarios tags each conformance scenario with a family.

Family Count Scenarios (index) safe-crossing 3 Safe Crossing (0), Parallel Paths (5), Bikes Only (6) standard-approach 5 Bike Approaches Ped (1), Speed Variant (8), Counter-Flow on Crosswalk (9), Cross-Street Cyclist (13), Overtake from Behind (16) high-speed 4 High-Speed Near Miss (2), Fast Approach (7), E-Scooter (14), Accelerating E-Bike (23) multi-agent 3 Multiple VRUs (3), Multi-Speed Converging (10), Dense Pedestrian Group (18) edge-case 3 Occluded Emergence (4), Stopped Pedestrian (12), Diagonal Jaywalker (19) accessibility 2 Wheelchair User (11), Child Pedestrian (15) non-linear 4 Cyclist Abort (17), Swerving Cyclist (20), Late Turn Toward Ped (21), U-Turn Cyclist (22)

docs.title: Braking profiles
docs.text:
Three scenarios set 'vehicle': 'ebike': Fast Approach, E-Scooter and Accelerating E-Bike. The other 21 use the default bicycle profile.

Profile Reaction time (s) Deceleration (m/s²) bicycle 0.84 1.96 ebike 0.84 6.0

The profile is applied twice. The danger model uses it to decide whether the cyclist can still stop, and make_pipeline passes the same values to the pipeline's speed-adaptive stopping distance. The sources of the values are listed in Safety model.

docs.title: Scoring
docs.text:
simulate_scenario steps a scenario at 30 FPS from t = 0 to its duration. Each frame gets a pipeline state and a ground-truth label with two tiers. A frame is a danger frame when the cyclist is on a collision course and cannot stop in time. It is also actionable when the time to collision is still longer than the pedestrian reaction time, so a warning can change the outcome.

Column Definition TP Frames in alert that are actionable. FN Actionable frames without alert. FP Frames in alert with no danger of either tier. TN Frames without alert and without danger. Sens TP divided by the number of actionable frames. Spec TN divided by the number of frames without danger. SevFN Severity-weighted miss rate: severity summed over missed actionable frames, divided by severity summed over all actionable frames. Lat Seconds from the first actionable frame to the first alert at or after it. WarnBgt Smallest time to closest approach, measured at each transition into alert. RxnAdq Share of those transitions that leave more than 1.87 s, the reaction time assumed for a distracted pedestrian. Fatigue Fraction of all frames spent in alert. Exp The scenario's expected_dominant. The testbench prints it and does not score against it.

Danger frames that are not actionable count on neither side: an alert during one is not a false positive, and silence during one is not a false negative.

The TOTAL row pools the frame counts over all scenarios before dividing. Its SevFN is the mean over the scenarios that have actionable frames.

  Alert fatigue (mean fraction of time in alert): 31.9%

Pooled over the suite, the default parameters alert on 91.9% of actionable frames and stay silent on 92.5% of frames without danger.

This invocation feeds the pipeline the scripted positions as they are. The paper's comparison table adds the fisheye localisation error, which python decision_testbench.py --compare applies unless --no-bbox-noise is given. Both runs are described in Testbench and Reproducing the paper.

A few rows need the scoring rules to read correctly. Occluded Emergence and Fast Approach show no true positives and no misses because they have no actionable frames. The pipeline does alert in both (10.7% and 23.0% of frames), 1.0 s and 1.6 s before closest approach, which is less than the 1.87 s a distracted pedestrian needs. Cyclist Abort expects safe as its dominant state and still contains 69 actionable frames before the cyclist turns away, all of which are caught.

docs.title: Extended suites
docs.text: The conformance suite is fixed by the paper. Scenarios written after it live in separate suites of bikeped.scenarios, so the published numbers stay reproducible while the library grows. This page describes the extended and stress suites and lists their scenarios.

docs.title: Working with a suite
docs.text:
python -m bikeped.scenarios list --suite extended
python -m bikeped.scenarios evaluate --suite extended

from bikeped.scenarios import get_suite

for scenario in get_suite('extended'):
    print(scenario['id'], scenario['family'], scenario['expected_dominant'])

Scenarios in these suites use the conformance format, so they run in the testbench, in the browser simulator and in the CARLA renderer without conversion. Per-agent model hints (child, wheelchair, e-scooter, cargo bike and so on) change only how the renderer draws an agent.

docs.title: extended
docs.text:
Forty-one hand-designed urban conflicts and deliberate negatives in twelve families. Speeds follow published ranges: walking 1.2 to 1.5 m/s, older adults 0.8 to 1.0, wheelchairs 1.0 to 1.3, commuter cyclists 4 to 7, fast road cyclists 8 to 11, e-scooters 5 to 7, cargo bikes 3.5 to 5.5.

Family Scenarios Covers turning 4 Turning conflicts occlusion 3 Occlusion and late emergence yielding 4 Yielding and braking cyclists counter-flow 2 Wrong-way and counter-flow riders shared-space 2 Shared space and sidewalk riding groups 5 Groups and platoons vulnerable 4 Vulnerable road users micromobility 4 Micromobility pedestrian-behaviour 5 Pedestrian behaviour near-miss 4 Near-miss geometry signal-platoon 1 Signal-phase platoons negative 3 True negatives

The dominant state of a run is the most severe state (alert > warning > safe > idle) that the pipeline holds for at least 0.3 s in total over the run. expected_dominant of an extended or stress scenario is the same rule applied to the per-frame labels of compute_ground_truth_danger rather than a judgement, and a test in tests/scenarios/ keeps the two in agreement. Scenarios that the default pipeline gets wrong keep their label and carry the tag known-hard: either the dominant state differs from the expected one, or the first alert comes more than 0.5 s after a danger interval begins. Fourteen scenarios carry it across the library: seven false alarms, five late alerts and two in the stress suite. They are the useful ones when you change the pipeline.

The ground truth is conservative. It labels a comfortable yield, a 2 m tangential pass and the whole ±3 s time-gap sweep of the generators as danger, so a yes in the table below means the pipeline agrees with a cautious reference rather than with a human judgement of the scene.

docs.title: Generators
docs.text: python -m bikeped.scenarios generate writes a seeded parametric suite to a JSON file. This page lists the families, explains what the seed controls, and shows how to load and evaluate the result.

docs.title: Command
docs.text:
python -m bikeped.scenarios generate --family time-gap --n 20 --seed 0 --out time-gap.json
Flag Default Meaning --family NAME required One of the six families below --n N 20 Number of scenarios --seed SEED 0 Seed of the jitter --out PATH - (stdout) Output JSON file

docs.title: Families
docs.text:
Family What is swept crossing-angle Pedestrian crossing angle from 30 to 150 degrees to the road cyclist-speed Cyclist speed from 3 to 11 m/s, arriving as the pedestrian is mid-lane time-gap Cyclist arrives -3 to +3 s relative to the pedestrian at the conflict point lateral-offset Cyclist passes 0 to 5 m to the side of the pedestrian group-size Groups of 1 to n pedestrians crossing together into one cyclist mixed-traffic Random mix of 1 to 4 pedestrians and 1 to 3 cyclists at random times

The first five are sweeps: the parameter is spread evenly over its range across the --n scenarios, so scenario k of a 20-scenario time-gap suite always has the same gap. The seed only adds small jitter, start times within 0.2 s and speeds within 5 %. mixed-traffic draws its agents from the seed. In every family the same family, n and seed give identical output.

expected_dominant is not chosen by hand: each generated scenario is labelled from the testbench ground truth (bikeped.scenarios.evaluate.label_scenario).

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
The file is a JSON list of scenarios in the usual format. Each one carries metadata that identifies how it was made:

$ python -m bikeped.scenarios generate --family time-gap --n 3 --seed 0 --out tg.json
wrote 3 scenarios to tg.json
Scenario id expected_dominant Time gap -3.0 s [time-gap s0 #0] time-gap-s0-000 alert Time gap +0.0 s [time-gap s0 #1] time-gap-s0-001 alert Time gap +3.0 s [time-gap s0 #2] time-gap-s0-002 alert

Every scenario in the file has suite set to generated-<family>, family set to the family, the tag generated and a one-sentence description, for example "The cyclist reaches the conflict point 3.0 s before the pedestrian."

docs.title: Using a generated suite
docs.text:
The file loads with json and runs through the testbench like any other scenario list:

import json
from decision_testbench import FisheyeCamera, PIPELINE_CONFIGS, simulate_scenario

suite = json.load(open('tg.json'))
cam = FisheyeCamera()
for scenario in suite:
    result = simulate_scenario(scenario, PIPELINE_CONFIGS['default'], cam=cam)

From Python, bikeped.scenarios.generators.generate(family, n, seed) returns the same list without writing a file.

docs.title: Simulation
docs.text:
The repository has three simulators that replay the same scripted scenarios through the same decision logic. This page says what each one models, what it needs to run, and which one to reach for.

All three read scenarios in the scenario format and evaluate them with DecisionPipeline from decision_pipeline.py, so a scenario behaves the same way in each. They differ in how much of the perception chain sits between the scripted positions and the pipeline.

  • Browser simulator

    A single HTML file. Plays a scenario in a bird's-eye view while the decision flowchart lights up, with sliders for camera placement and detector uncertainty.

  • Offline testbench

    decision_testbench.py scores every scenario against ground-truth danger labels and prints the tables reported in the paper. sim_visualizer.py renders the same runs as schematic fisheye videos.

  • CARLA renderer

    python -m bikeped.sim places the scripted agents at a crosswalk in a CARLA town and records photorealistic video with per-frame ground truth.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Browser simulator Offline testbench CARLA renderer Entry point simulator/index.html python decision_testbench.py, python sim_visualizer.py python -m bikeped.sim render Needs A browser Python 3.10+ and requirements.txt A CARLA server (UE4 or UE5 build), the carla wheel and a GPU Perception model Adjustable detector recall, latency and tracker settings Calibrated fisheye projection, bounding-box localisation error, size-aware detection drops, track persistence Rendered images. The scripted positions drive the pipeline, the renderer supplies pixels and boxes Ground truth Expected dominant state per scenario Per-frame danger assessment from the braking model Per-frame danger assessment plus 2D and 3D boxes per camera view Output On-screen only Metric tables on stdout, latency_sweep.json, figures in paper/, MP4s from sim_visualizer.py A run directory with manifest.json, videos, ground-truth JSONL and stills Deterministic Yes, unless detection drops are enabled Yes. Monte Carlo trials are seeded by trial index Scripted agents are; rendering and ambient traffic depend on the server Typical use Explaining the logic, trying a camera position, comparing decision rules by eye Reproducing the paper, tuning parameters, regression checks Producing video and labelled frames for detector work and demos

docs.title: Which one to use
docs.text:
Start in the browser when the question is "what does the pipeline do in this situation". It runs with no install, and switching between the seven pipeline variants takes one click.

Use the testbench when the answer has to be a number. It is the only simulator that scores alerts against the ground-truth danger model described in Safety model, and every table in the paper comes from it. Reproduce the paper lists the commands.

Use CARLA when pixels matter: checking how a scenario looks through the deployed lens, exporting labelled frames, or producing video. The renderer does not replace the testbench for metrics. It records the decision state and the danger label next to each frame so the two can be compared afterwards.

docs.title: Shared pieces
docs.text: Piece Where it lives Used by Decision logic decision_pipeline.py Testbench and CARLA renderer import it. The browser simulator carries a JavaScript port Conformance scenarios decision_testbench.SCENARIOS All three. docs.title: Browser simulator
docs.text:
The browser simulator runs the decision pipeline on the scenario suites in a bird's eye view, one frame at a time, with no install. This page describes its controls and how its numbers relate to the offline testbench.

Open the simulator. From a checkout, open simulator/index.html in any browser; it is a single self-contained HTML file, and simulator/scenarios.extended.js next to it adds the suites beyond conformance.

docs.title: Panels
docs.text: Panel Contents Bird's eye view Road, crosswalk, cameras with their field of view, agents and their tracks, in the scenario frame Decision pipeline A flowchart of the stages (detection, classification and ground projection, tracking, then the three decision checks) with the active path lit and the current output: idle blue, safe green, warning orange, alert red blink Timeline Scenario time, duration, play, reset, loop and a speed slider Telemetry Number of objects, number of tracks and the minimum bike-pedestrian distance Systematic error budget The localisation error that the chosen camera setup and uncertainty parameters introduce for the scenario being played

docs.title: Suites and scenarios
docs.text:
The suite bar along the top switches between suites. Conformance holds the paper's 24 scenarios and is always present. Further suites (extended, stress) appear when scenarios.extended.js is present next to the page; without it the page runs with the conformance suite alone.

Selecting a scenario writes its slug into the URL fragment, so a link such as simulator/#fast-approach opens that scenario directly. Other pages of these docs use this to link to individual scenarios.

docs.title: Pipeline variants
docs.text:
The pipeline selector offers seven configurations. The first is the deployed configuration; the last three are the decision-rule baselines from the paper, run with the same front end.

Variant Memory (frames) d_min (m) d_max (m) Min displacement (m) Lookback (frames) Speed-adaptive Rule Selected 58 1.9 24.8 0.147 2 yes pairwise Conservative 60 1.5 15.0 0.05 3 no pairwise Speed-Adaptive 60 1.0 20.0 0.05 2 yes pairwise Proximity Only 0 2.0 10.0 0.1 3 no pairwise Distance Only 58 1.9 10.0 0.0 2 no distance_only Naive Closing 58 1.9 24.8 0.147 2 yes naive_closing TTC 58 1.9 24.8 0.0 2 yes ttc, threshold 3 s

The values are written into the page and mirror decision_testbench.PIPELINE_CONFIGS. Decision pipeline explains each parameter and rule.

docs.title: Cameras
docs.text: The setup buttons place cameras in four presets: single pole, cross-cam (a second pole at (5, 13) facing the first across the crosswalk), centre and overhead. The + and − buttons add and remove cameras, and the sliders set the selected camera's position (X, Y), height, field of view and heading. The default camera stands at (5, −13) m, 5.5 m high, with a 220° field of view facing the crosswalk.

docs.title: Uncertainty parameters
docs.text:
The uncertainty panel sets the detector and tracker model that turns ground truth into noisy observations:

Group Parameters YOLO detection Average recall and precision for small, medium and large objects (COCO size buckets), latency, high and low confidence thresholds BEV projection Ground tilt uncertainty (the street is not perfectly level) ByteTrack Kalman filter Position and velocity noise, frames before a lost track is dropped, IoU threshold, frame rate

Changing them changes how often agents drop out and how far their projected positions wander, which is the quickest way to see why the decision stages need memory and a lookback.

docs.title: Relation to the testbench
docs.text: The simulator is a JavaScript port written for inspection. The numbers in the paper and on these pages come from the Python offline testbench, which shares its code with the deployed system. Use the simulator to understand a scenario and the testbench to measure one.

docs.title: Offline testbench
docs.text:
decision_testbench.py replays scripted scenarios through a model of the camera, the detector and the tracker, feeds the result to the decision pipeline, and scores every frame against a ground-truth danger label. This page describes that loop, the metrics it prints, the command-line flags, and the companion video renderer sim_visualizer.py.

$ python decision_testbench.py
Loaded calibration: FOV=197.90 cx=1752.7 cy=1804.5 f=1013.3 R=1750 frame=3500x3500 pad=3840 pitch=0 k1=0 k2=0
Running all scenarios with Default pipeline...

  Scenario                       TP   FP   FN   TN   Sens   Spec  SevFN    Lat WarnBgt RxnAdq Fatigue       Exp
  Safe Crossing                   0    0    0  196  0.0% 100.0%  0.0%    N/A     N/A    N/A   0.0%      safe
  Bike Approaches Ped            86   25   14  101 86.0% 80.2% 26.3%   0.47    3.5s   100%  49.1%     alert

...

The excerpt drops the rule lines and 21 scenario rows. Run from the repository root so that config.yaml and camera_calibration.json are found.

docs.title: What happens in one frame
docs.text:
simulate_scenario steps a scenario at 30 frames per second from t = 0 to the last waypoint. At each step it does the following, in this order:

  1. Interpolates every agent's scripted position at time t. An agent outside its path's time span is absent.
  2. Drops detections at random, in Monte Carlo runs only. The recall comes from the projected bounding-box area of the agent on the fisheye sensor, so small, distant agents are missed more often. The drop pattern is independent per frame (iid) or bursty (gilbert).
  3. Replaces the true position with the position the deployed system would compute, when localisation error is on. compute_bbox_error projects the agent's 3D box through the calibrated lens, takes the bottom centre of the resulting 2D box and projects it back to the ground.
  4. Delays the detections by camera_delay_frames through a ring buffer, when a latency is being simulated.
  5. Passes them through GroundPlaneTracker, which keeps a track alive for up to one second of missed detections using constant-velocity prediction, and optionally forecasts positions forward to compensate for the delay.
  6. Converts positions to camera-relative coordinates and calls DecisionPipeline.evaluate, which returns idle, safe, warning or alert.
  7. Computes the ground-truth danger assessment for time t from the scripted positions.

Steps 2 to 5 are described in Perception and Detection and localisation uncertainty, step 6 in Decision pipeline, and step 7 in Safety model.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Ground truth has two tiers. A frame is actionable when there is danger and a warning could still help. A danger frame that is no longer actionable counts neither for nor against the system.

Column Definition TP Frames in alert that are actionable danger frames FN Actionable danger frames without an alert FP Frames in alert with no danger of either tier TN Frames without an alert and without danger Sens TP divided by the number of actionable frames Spec TN divided by the number of safe frames SevFN Severity summed over missed actionable frames, divided by severity summed over all actionable frames Lat Seconds from the first actionable frame to the first alert at or after it WarnBgt Smallest warning budget over the alert onsets of the scenario. The budget is the time from an onset to the closest approach RxnAdq Share of alert onsets with a budget above 1.87 s, the reaction time assumed for a distracted pedestrian Fatigue Fraction of all frames spent in alert Exp The scenario's expected_dominant state, printed for reference

The TOTAL row pools frames over scenarios for the four counts, sensitivity and specificity. Its SevFN is the mean of the per-scenario rates over scenarios that contain actionable frames. A scenario with no actionable frames, such as Safe Crossing, shows 0.0% sensitivity and does not enter the pooled figure.

simulate_scenario returns the same quantities as a dictionary (sensitivity, specificity, sev_weighted_fn_rate, alert_latency_s, min_warning_budget_s, mean_warning_budget_s, reaction_adequacy, alert_fraction, peak_severity, peak_bike_speed_ms) together with the per-frame arrays times, states, dangers and assessments.

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
One mode runs per invocation. If several mode flags are given, the first in this table wins.

The run without flags is the one case that leaves localisation error off, which is why its totals above match the default block of --no-bbox-noise --compare and not that of --compare.

docs.title: Scenario videos with sim_visualizer.py
docs.text:
sim_visualizer.py renders the scenarios as the pole camera would see them: agents drawn as 3D boxes and projected through the fisheye model onto a ground grid. It runs the same pipeline as the testbench and writes one MP4 per scenario into the working directory.

python sim_visualizer.py --no-display                  # all scenarios, headless
python sim_visualizer.py --scenarios 1 5 7             # by index, with a preview window
python sim_visualizer.py --scenarios 7 --errors --no-display
Option Default Meaning --scenarios I [I ...] all Zero-based indices into SCENARIOS --pipeline NAME optimized Key of PIPELINE_CONFIGS --fps N 30 Simulation and video frame rate --two-cam off Also render a side-by-side view with a second camera across the road --height M, --pitch DEG 3.6576 m, automatic Mounting geometry, see Camera placement --errors off Run the pipeline on error-perturbed positions, draw the error vectors, and save a JSON log of observations --no-save off Do not write the MP4 --no-display off Do not open the OpenCV preview window. Required on a machine without a display

Each frame is 1080 by 1080 pixels and shows:

  • the ground grid at 2 m spacing and the crosswalk, as the lens distorts them;
  • the part of the image circle that falls outside the 3840 by 2160 sensor, dimmed;
  • each agent with its trail, and a line between every cyclist and pedestrian closer than prox_max;
  • the scenario name, the time, and a badge with the current decision state;
  • during danger, the severity, cyclist speed, time to collision and stopping distance from the ground-truth model;
  • a 300 by 300 pixel top-down inset in the lower right corner.

Files are named sim_<index>_<scenario name>.mp4, for example sim_01_bike_approaches_ped.mp4. With --errors the name gains _errors and a sidecar ..._observations.json holds the per-frame true and observed positions.

docs.title: CARLA renderer
docs.text: bikeped.sim plays a scenario from the scenario library in a CARLA world and records what a camera at the intersection would see, together with the decision state and ground-truth boxes for every frame. One command line drives both engine generations: Unreal Engine 4 (CARLA 0.9.14 to 0.9.16) and Unreal Engine 5 (CARLA 0.10.0).

docs.title: How a render runs
docs.text:
The runner connects to a CARLA server and puts the world in synchronous mode with a fixed step of 1 / fps seconds, so simulated time advances only when the runner ticks. It maps the scenario frame onto a crosswalk from crosswalks.json, spawns one actor per scripted agent and one CARLA sensor per camera view, then steps through the scenario. On every tick it moves the agents along their scripted paths, reads back the simulated poses and images, evaluates the decision pipeline and the ground-truth danger label, and passes a FrameRecord to the Recorder. When the scenario ends, or the run fails, the session destroys the actors it spawned and restores the world settings.

Data flow of one CARLA render, from the scenario to the files in the run directory Scenario bikeped.scenarios paths, models, hints Runner session, actors, camera rigs one tick advances 1 / fps seconds FrameRecord agent poses, camera models, images one per tick spawn, move, tick poses, images CARLA server UE4 (0.9.14 to 0.9.16) or UE5 (0.10.0) synchronous mode Decision and danger label DecisionPipeline.evaluate compute_ground_truth_danger Recorder writes the run directory renders/<run_id>/ manifest.json video/*.mp4 gt/*.jsonl stills/ One render: the runner drives the server tick by tick and the recorder writes the run directory.

The decision pipeline and the danger model read the scripted positions (sx, sy in the scenario frame), so the state shown in the overlay does not depend on how closely a simulated actor followed its path. The gap between the scripted and the simulated position is stored for every agent as track_error_m.

docs.title: UE4 and UE5
docs.text:
UE4 UE5 CARLA releases 0.9.14 to 0.9.16 0.10.0 Launcher script CarlaUE4.sh CarlaUnreal.sh Python client wheels Python 3.10 to 3.12 cp310 only (Python 3.10) Rendering Unreal Engine 4 Unreal Engine 5 with Lumen and Nanite Maps Town01 to Town15, Town10HD_Opt by default Town10HD_Opt and Mine_01 Actor catalogue Full set of two-wheelers and walkers, wheelchair walkers on 0.9.16 Four-wheeled vehicles and walkers; no rideable two-wheeler, cyclists need --cyclist-proxy walker Validation Developed and run end to end against CARLA 0.9.16 Tested against an in-memory stand-in for the 0.10.0 API; not yet run against a real 0.10.0 server (current limits) Install root variable CARLA_UE4_ROOT CARLA_UE5_ROOT --engine value ue4 ue5

The two lines differ in what they can spawn, so the renderer asks the server instead of assuming. python -m bikeped.sim probe reports the engine, the versions, the available maps and the capabilities the actor code depends on. Setup for each line is on its own page: UE4 and UE5.

docs.title: A minimal session
docs.text:
export CARLA_UE4_ROOT=/path/to/CARLA_0.9.16   # directory that holds CarlaUE4.sh

python -m bikeped.sim server --engine ue4     # terminal 1, keeps running
python -m bikeped.sim probe                   # terminal 2, check the connection
python -m bikeped.sim render --scenario fast-approach --rig pole,fisheye

The render writes renders/ue4_fast-approach_clear_noon/: a manifest, one video per view, per-frame ground truth and a few key stills. The layout is described in Run output.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command What it does python -m bikeped.sim probe Connects to a server and prints engine, version, maps and capabilities python -m bikeped.sim server Starts a CARLA server from CARLA_UE4_ROOT or CARLA_UE5_ROOT python -m bikeped.sim presets Lists the weather, rig and quality presets python -m bikeped.sim render Renders one scenario, a suite, or every scenario python -m bikeped.sim export Converts the ground truth of a finished run to COCO or YOLO

Every flag is listed in the CLI reference.

docs.title: Actors
docs.text: This page describes how the agents of a scenario become CARLA actors, how they follow their scripted paths, and what happens when the server lacks a blueprint. The code is in bikeped/sim/actors.py.

docs.title: From agent to actor
docs.text:
A scenario agent has a type, which is what the decision pipeline uses, and an optional model, which only changes how it looks. A person becomes a walker. A bike becomes a two-wheeled vehicle with a rider, or a walker standing in for the cyclist on engines without one (see below).

{'type': 'bike', 'id': 2, 'model': 'ebike', 'label': 'e-bike',
 'path': [{'x': 34, 'y': 2, 't': 0}, {'x': 5, 'y': 0, 't': 4}]}

docs.title: Walkers
docs.text:
Walker blueprints are the server's walker.pedestrian.* blueprints, sorted by id, and one is drawn with the run's seed.

model Blueprint pool adult (default), runner Walkers whose age attribute is not child child Walkers with age = child, or the adult pool if there are none wheelchair Walkers with can_use_wheelchair = true, spawned in a wheelchair; the adult pool if the server has none (CARLA 0.9.16 has them)

docs.title: Two-wheelers
docs.text:
For a bike agent the renderer keeps the vehicle blueprints the server reports as two-wheelers and takes the first entry of the model's preference list that exists:

model Preferred blueprints, in order bicycle (default) vehicle.bh.crossbike, vehicle.gazelle.omafiets, vehicle.diamondback.century road_bike vehicle.diamondback.century, vehicle.bh.crossbike ebike vehicle.bh.crossbike, vehicle.gazelle.omafiets cargo_bike vehicle.gazelle.omafiets, vehicle.bh.crossbike escooter vehicle.vespa.zx125, vehicle.bh.crossbike moped vehicle.vespa.zx125, vehicle.yamaha.yzf, vehicle.kawasaki.ninja

If none of them exists, it picks a random two-wheeler whose base_type is bicycle, and failing that any two-wheeler. The blueprint that was spawned is stored per agent in the manifest as blueprint, next to the requested model, so a dataset built from renders can be filtered by what is actually in the image.

The model changes pixels only. The decision pipeline treats every bike alike, and the braking profile of the danger label comes from the scenario's vehicle key (Safety model).

docs.title: Drive modes
docs.text:
--drive selects how actors follow their paths. The default is kinematic.

Mode How the actor moves kinematic The actor is placed on its scripted pose every tick. Height comes from a ground profile sampled before any actor exists, yaw from the smoothed heading and, for two-wheelers, roll from the lean angle. Walkers also get a WalkerControl so the walk cycle plays. velocity Walkers are steered with WalkerControl (the scripted velocity plus a proportional correction on position error). Riders get target linear and angular velocities plus a light throttle and steer, so wheels, pedals and handlebars move. An actor is put back on its scripted pose only when its position error exceeds a tolerance.

Under velocity the simulated actor can drift from the script, for example where a path turns sharply. The runner stores that drift per agent and frame as track_error_m, the ground-plane distance in metres between the scripted and the simulated position.

Positions reported to the decision pipeline and to the danger model always come from the script, in both modes. Drift moves the actor in the image, and therefore the ground-truth boxes, which describe the simulated actor.

docs.title: Engines without a rideable two-wheeler
docs.text: CARLA 0.10.0 ships no rideable bicycle or motorcycle blueprint. On such a server render refuses a scenario with bike agents unless --cyclist-proxy walker is passed. With the flag, a walker follows each cyclist's scripted path and the manifest records the substitution. Pedestrian-only scenarios are unaffected. python -m bikeped.sim probe shows in advance whether the server has a rideable two-wheeler; UE5 setup has the details.

docs.title: Ambient actors
docs.text: Actors added by --ambient carry role: "ambient" and have no scenario path; the simulator drives them. See Environment.
