docs.title: Cameras
docs.text: A render can record several views of the same run. This page lists the views, explains how the fisheye view is built from cube faces so that it matches the deployed lens, and documents the camera model that ties pixels to world coordinates.

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
Select views with --rig, a comma-separated list. Each view is written to video/<view>.mp4 in the run directory.

View Kind What it shows pole pinhole Camera on the pole at the testbench camera position (12 ft), aimed so the crosswalk and every scripted path fit in the frame fisheye fisheye The deployed lens on the pole, rendered as cube faces and resampled through the calibrated model chase pinhole Follows the first cyclist (or pedestrian, if there is no cyclist) from behind and above orbit pinhole Slow eye-level arc around the conflict point with a longer lens street pinhole Static eye-level tripod on the kerb bev pinhole Straight down from 60 m with a narrow lens, image up along scenario +y

pole, fisheye, street and bev are static. chase and orbit move their sensor before every tick. The default is --rig pole. The schematic top-down panel used by the split and quad layouts is drawn separately from the scenario coordinates and is not a CARLA view.

python -m bikeped.sim render --scenario fast-approach --rig pole,fisheye,bev

docs.title: The fisheye view
docs.text:
The calibrated field of view is 197.9°, so the image circle reaches 98.95° from the optical axis. The deployed camera is level (camera.pitch_deg is 0) and faces across the road, so the image circle covers more than a hemisphere in front of it. A CARLA RGB camera is a pinhole and cannot cover that, so the renderer captures 90° cube faces from the pole position and resamples them through the lens model.

Five cube faces are remapped through the calibrated lens model into one fisheye frame Cube faces up left front right down one 90° pinhole camera per face Lens model θ: angle from the optical axis r = f (θ + k1 θ³ + k2 θ⁵) f, k1, k2 from camera_calibration.json FisheyeRemap.remap(face_images) Fisheye frame 3840 × 2160 sensor crop 3500 px image circle, clipped top and bottom Cube faces rendered by CARLA are resampled into the frame the deployed lens would produce.
  1. deployed_fisheye_model(position, yaw_deg) builds a CameraModel of kind fisheye from camera_calibration.json and config.yaml: an equidistant projection with the k1 and k2 terms and f = radius / (fov / 2) (the focal length the testbench uses), a 3500 px image circle on a 3840 × 2160 sensor, and the pitch from camera.pitch_deg. A testbench heading h corresponds to CARLA yaw -h, so the testbench default heading of 90° is yaw_deg=-90.
  2. FisheyeRemap(model, face_size=1024, supersample=1) works out which cube faces the image circle needs. For the deployed lens remap.faces is ('down', 'front', 'right', 'left', 'up'); the face behind the camera receives no pixels and is not rendered.
  3. remap.face_camera(face) returns a 90° pinhole CameraModel for a face, and the rig spawns one CARLA camera from each.
  4. On every tick remap.remap(face_images) returns the BGR fisheye frame. Pixels outside the image circle are black.

The lens parameters come from the calibration file that the deployed system reads:

Parameter Value Unit Source Projection equidistant, r = f (θ + k1 θ³ + k2 θ⁵) camera_calibration.json focal_length 1013.31 px per radian camera_calibration.json fov_deg 197.9 degrees camera_calibration.json radius_px 1750 px camera_calibration.json k1, k2 0.0, 0.0 camera_calibration.json Camera height 3.6576 m config.yaml, camera.height

The fisheye CameraModel has to agree with decision_testbench.FisheyeCamera.world_to_pixel to sub-pixel accuracy. That agreement is what lets a rendered fisheye frame stand in for a frame from the deployed camera: a ground point lands on the same pixel in both.

docs.title: Camera model
docs.text:
Every view is described by a CameraModel (bikeped/sim/types.py). The models of a run are stored in its manifest, so boxes can be re-projected later without a server.

Field Default Meaning name View name, for example pole kind pinhole or fisheye width, height Image size in pixels position Camera position in the CARLA world frame, metres forward, right, up Orthonormal basis vectors in the world frame fov_deg 90.0 Pinhole: horizontal field of view. Fisheye: full field of view of the image circle cx, cy image centre Principal point in pixels f_px_per_rad Fisheye focal length in pixels per radian k1, k2 0.0 Odd polynomial terms of the fisheye model circle_radius_px Radius of the fisheye image circle

A world point P has camera coordinates (f, r, u) = (forward · d, right · d, up · d) with d = P - position. Image u grows with r and image v grows with -u. For a pinhole view the focal length in pixels is width / (2 tan(fov / 2)). The world frame is CARLA's: left-handed, x forward, y right, z up, with rotations given as (pitch, yaw, roll) in degrees.

bikeped.sim.projection converts between the two descriptions and projects points:

from bikeped.sim.projection import carla_rotation_to_basis, project_points

forward, right, up = carla_rotation_to_basis(pitch=-10.0, yaw=90.0, roll=0.0)
uv, valid, depth = project_points(points_world, camera)   # (N, 2), (N,) bool, (N,)

docs.title: Layout and overlay
docs.text:
Each view is saved twice: clean as video/<view>.mp4, and with the heads-up display as video/<view>_overlay.mp4. --no-overlay skips the second file. --layout chooses how the views and the top-down panel are arranged in video/composite.mp4:

Layout Composite single The first view alone split The first view on the left and the top-down panel in a square on the right quad A 2 × 2 grid with up to three views and the top-down panel in the last cell. Without the panel, a fourth view takes that cell

The first view is the primary one. Views are scaled to fit their cell and centred on the background. They are never stretched, so a fisheye frame keeps its aspect ratio next to a 16:9 view.

docs.title: Quality presets
docs.text:
--quality takes draft, standard (the default) or cinematic and trades render time for image quality:

Preset Pinhole views Fisheye cube face Fisheye output Post-processing draft 960 × 540 512 px 0.25 × the 3840 × 2160 sensor Motion blur, bloom and lens flare off standard 1920 × 1080 1024 px 0.5 × sensor (1920 × 1080) Light motion blur and bloom cinematic 2560 × 1440 1536 px 0.5 × sensor Stronger motion blur and bloom, lens flare, chromatic aberration

The values are QUALITY_PRESETS in bikeped/sim/rigs.py; python -m bikeped.sim presets prints the sizes. The fisheye view renders one camera per cube face, so it is the view that gains most from draft while a setup is being checked.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text: This page covers where a scenario is placed in the CARLA world and under which conditions it is rendered: map, crosswalk, weather, ambient traffic, seed and frame rate.

docs.title: Map
docs.text: --map loads a map before the render if the server has a different one open. Without it the renderer keeps whatever map is loaded, which on a freshly started server is Town10HD_Opt on both engine lines.

docs.title: Crosswalks
docs.text:
Scenarios are written in the scenario frame: metres, x along the road, y across it, crosswalk centre at (5, 0). To place a scenario in a town, the renderer anchors that frame on a real crosswalk taken from crosswalks.json in the repository root. The file lists the 16 crosswalks of Town10HD_Opt, and --crosswalk picks one by index. The default is 4. On any other map the renderer reads the crosswalk polygons from the live map instead (world.get_map().get_crosswalks()), and --crosswalks-file points at another file in the same format.

Each entry has these fields:

Field Unit Meaning id Index used by --crosswalk center m [x, y, z] of the crosswalk centre in the CARLA world frame corners m Four [x, y, z] corners of the crosswalk polygon width_m m Length of the short side, measured along the road length_m m Length of the long side, the distance a pedestrian crosses road_heading_deg degrees Heading of the road at the crosswalk

The crosswalk centre becomes scenario (5, 0). Scenario +y runs along the crosswalk, the direction pedestrians walk, and scenario +x runs along the road, the direction cyclists ride. The pole camera stands where the testbench puts it, at scenario (5, -13) and 3.6576 m (12 ft) high, read from decision_testbench.FisheyeCamera.

The 16 crosswalks of Town10HD_Opt id Centre (x, y) width_m length_m road_heading_deg 0 (-46.9, 118.5) 2.5 18.9 -179.7 1 (42.2, 58.5) 3.1 17.8 179.5 2 (-46.8, -47.9) 2.6 19.4 0.2 3 (-31.2, -62.9) 2.6 18.7 -90.1 4 (-46.9, 36.5) 2.9 22.2 0.1 5 (-47.3, 3.0) 2.6 20.6 -179.7 6 (-62.7, -63.3) 2.5 18.3 91.0 7 (104.4, 2.0) 2.5 18.7 -179.1 8 (87.5, 20.8) 2.6 24.3 90.6 9 (103.8, 37.4) 2.8 19.8 0.0 10 (91.3, 68.1) 3.0 17.0 90.2 11 (-93.1, 20.3) 2.6 25.7 -89.5 12 (-108.7, 39.0) 2.5 18.9 0.4 13 (-107.7, 3.5) 2.9 20.3 -179.3 14 (42.2, 35.1) 3.5 20.3 -0.3 15 (-30.6, 67.9) 2.5 13.0 -90.5

Values are rounded from crosswalks.json.

docs.title: Extracting crosswalks from another map
docs.text:
tools/carla_find_crosswalks.py reads the crosswalk polygons of the map a running server has loaded and writes them in the same format:

python tools/carla_find_crosswalks.py --map Town10HD_Opt --export crosswalks.json
python tools/carla_find_crosswalks.py --goto 4        # move the spectator to crosswalk 4

Use --goto to look at a candidate in the simulator window before rendering on it.

docs.title: Weather
docs.text:
--weather takes one of nine presets. A scenario can also carry a hint in its render block, for example 'render': {'weather': 'wet_night'}, which is used when the flag is not given.

$ python -m bikeped.sim presets
weather
  clear_noon   sun    60 deg, clouds 10, rain 0, fog 0
  golden_hour  sun     9 deg, clouds 20, rain 0, fog 3
  overcast     sun    45 deg, clouds 90, rain 0, fog 5
  light_rain   sun    35 deg, clouds 80, rain 30, fog 8
  heavy_rain   sun    30 deg, clouds 100, rain 90, fog 20
  dusk         sun    -3 deg, clouds 40, rain 0, fog 5, street lights on
  clear_night  sun   -40 deg, clouds 10, rain 0, fog 0, street lights on
  wet_night    sun   -40 deg, clouds 70, rain 10, fog 6, street lights on
  fog          sun    25 deg, clouds 60, rain 0, fog 45

The sun angle is the altitude. The sun's azimuth is set relative to the pole camera's viewing direction rather than as an absolute angle, so the pole view is lit from behind or from the side whatever the orientation of the crosswalk. Fields that a server does not know are skipped, so the same presets serve CARLA 0.9.x and 0.10.0. Without --weather and without a hint the preset is clear_noon.

The weather name is the last part of the run id, so renders of one scenario under different conditions land in separate directories. python -m bikeped.sim presets prints the presets with their parameters.

docs.title: Ambient traffic
docs.text:
--ambient adds background vehicles and walkers that are not part of the scenario. The table gives the number of actors requested per level.

Level Vehicles Walkers none 0 0 light 6 8 busy 20 24

Spawning is best effort: a map without spawn points or a full navigation mesh leaves fewer ambient actors and a log message, and never stops the render. Ambient actors are kept out of the scripted corridor, which is the bounding box of all scripted paths plus a margin. Vehicles spawn outside it, drive under CARLA's Traffic Manager, and are stopped when they approach the corridor. Walkers spawn on the navigation mesh outside the corridor, do not cross the road, and are sent back to where they started if they wander in. The street looks inhabited and the scripted encounter plays out undisturbed.

docs.title: Seed and frame rate
docs.text: --seed (default 0) fixes every random choice of a run, such as which walker blueprint an agent gets and where ambient traffic spawns. --fps (default 30) sets both the video frame rate and the simulation step: the world runs in synchronous mode with a fixed step of 1 / fps seconds, so a render takes as long as it takes and the result does not depend on how fast the machine is.

docs.title: Ground truth
docs.text: Every rendered frame comes with the state of each agent, its box in each view, and the danger label of the safety model. This page lists those records and shows how to export them for detector training.

docs.title: Per-frame records
docs.text:
The runner builds one FrameRecord per tick. It holds the frame index, the time t in seconds, the decision state, the alerting pair if there is one, the danger assessment, and one AgentState per agent.

AgentState field Unit Meaning id Agent id from the scenario kind person or bike sx, sy m Scripted position in the scenario frame heading Scripted heading in the scenario frame speed m/s Scripted ground speed location m Centre of the simulated actor's 3D box, CARLA world frame rotation degrees (pitch, yaw, roll) of the box extent m Half sizes of the box along the actor's forward, right and up axes role scripted or ambient model Rendering hint from the scenario blueprint CARLA blueprint id that was spawned track_error_m m Ground-plane distance between scripted and simulated position

docs.title: Boxes per view
docs.text:
project_box(agent, camera) projects the eight corners of an agent's oriented 3D box into a view and returns None when the agent is outside it. frame_ground_truth(frame, view) does this for every agent of a frame.

Field Meaning id, kind, role Copied from the agent bbox [x1, y1, x2, y2] in pixels, the 2D box around the projected 3D box corners_image The eight projected corners, an 8 × 2 array distance_m Distance from the camera to the agent truncation Fraction of the box that falls outside the image visible_fraction Fraction of the agent that is not occluded, when the view has a depth or instance buffer

Pinhole boxes are clipped against the near plane edge by edge. An agent that straddles the camera plane keeps a correct box, where dropping the corners behind the camera would shrink it. Fisheye boxes go through the lens model, so they follow the distortion of the image.

from bikeped.sim.groundtruth import frame_ground_truth

for obj in frame_ground_truth(frame, "pole"):
    print(obj["id"], obj["kind"], obj["bbox"], round(obj["distance_m"], 1))

The same records are written to gt/<view>.jsonl, one JSON object per frame:

{"index": 0, "t": 0.0, "width": 1920, "height": 1080, "objects": [{"id": 1, "kind": "person", "role": "scripted", "bbox": [...], "corners_image": [...], "distance_m": ..., "truncation": ..., "visible_fraction": ...}]}

visible_fraction is null when the view has no depth or instance buffer. The runner attaches those buffers to the pole view only, when the server offers depth and instance cameras, so the other views carry boxes without a visibility estimate.

docs.title: Danger label
docs.text:
FrameRecord.danger is the result of decision_testbench.compute_ground_truth_danger(scenario, t), the kinematic safety model that labels every number in the paper. It is evaluated on the scripted paths.

Field Unit Meaning is_danger The cyclist is on a collision course and cannot stop in time, or time to collision is low actionable is_danger, and a warning can still change the outcome severity 0 to 1 Grows with the square of the cyclist's speed ttc s Time to collision, infinite when there is none d_min_future m Minimum future distance within the lookahead closing_speed m/s Positive when approaching bike_speed m/s Cyclist ground speed stopping_dist m Distance the cyclist needs to stop warning_budget s Warning time left before closest approach distance m Current distance of the pair

Safety model explains how these are derived.

docs.title: Export to COCO or YOLO
docs.text:
python -m bikeped.sim export renders/ue4_fast-approach_clear_noon --format coco
python -m bikeped.sim export renders/ue4_fast-approach_clear_noon --format yolo --view fisheye
Flag Default Meaning RUN_DIR A finished run directory --format coco or yolo --view pole View whose boxes and frames are exported --out inside RUN_DIR Annotation file (COCO) or dataset folder (YOLO)

The exporters turn one view of a run into a detection dataset with the classes person and bicycle. They read manifest.json and gt/<view>.jsonl, so they need no server.

COCO YOLO Output One annotation file and an images folder next to it A folder with images/, labels/ and data.yaml Box [x, y, width, height] in pixels, origin at the top-left corner class cx cy w h, centre and size divided by the image width and height Classes person is id 1, bicycle is id 2 person is 0, bicycle is 1

Images are copied from the saved frames when the run has them. Without saved frames they are decoded from the clean video of the view, whose frame k belongs to line k of the ground-truth file. YOLO file names carry the run id, so several runs can be exported into one folder, and a frame without boxes gets an empty label file and counts as a negative.

The Python functions take filters that the defaults leave off:

from bikeped.sim.export import export_coco, export_yolo

run = "renders/ue4_fast-approach_clear_noon"
export_coco(run, "dataset/annotations.json", view="pole", min_visible=0.3, every=5)
export_yolo(run, "dataset_yolo", view="fisheye", min_area=64.0)
Argument Default Meaning min_visible 0.0 Drop boxes whose visible_fraction is known and below this value. Boxes without a visibility estimate are kept min_area 0.0 Drop boxes smaller than this area in square pixels every 1 Export every n-th frame

docs.title: Run output
docs.text: Each render writes one directory. This page describes its files and the structure of manifest.json.

docs.title: Directory layout
docs.text:
renders/<run_id>/
  manifest.json                 run metadata, camera models, per-frame records
  video/<view>.mp4              clean view, H.264
  video/<view>_overlay.mp4      view with the heads-up display
  video/composite.mp4           the layout chosen with --layout
  frames/<view>/000000.jpg      individual frames, only with --save-frames
  gt/<view>.jsonl               one line per frame: boxes per agent
  stills/                       first frame, first alert frame, closest approach

The run id is <engine>_<scenario-id>_<weather>, for example ue4_fast-approach_clear_noon. --out changes the parent directory, which defaults to renders.

docs.title: Videos
docs.text:
File Content video/<view>.mp4 The view as rendered, without any drawing on top. Use it as detector input video/<view>_overlay.mp4 The same frames with the heads-up display: decision state, agent boxes and the danger indicator. Not written with --no-overlay video/composite.mp4 The views arranged as single, split or quad

Videos are encoded at the frame rate given by --fps, with ffmpeg (libx264, yuv420p) through a pipe. When no ffmpeg executable is found, the recorder falls back to OpenCV's mp4v codec and logs a warning; those files play in most players but are not H.264.

docs.title: Frames
docs.text: --save-frames jpg or --save-frames png additionally writes every frame of every view to frames/<view>/, numbered from 000000. The default is none. The COCO and YOLO exporters copy saved frames when they exist and otherwise decode the frames from the clean video.

docs.title: Stills
docs.text: stills/ holds a few frames picked from the run: the first frame, the first frame in which the pipeline is in alert, and the frame of closest approach between a cyclist and a pedestrian.

docs.title: manifest.json
docs.text:
The manifest is one JSON object with these top-level keys:

Key Contents run_id <engine>_<scenario-id>_<weather> run Run metadata (RunInfo, below) scenario The scenario dict that was rendered, with its metadata layout, overlay, views Composite layout, whether HUD videos were written, rendered views cameras The CameraModel of each view as a dict, see Cameras videos Video files by name, relative to the run directory frames_dir, frame_ext Folder and extension of saved frames, or null without --save-frames gt Ground-truth file per view, gt/<view>.jsonl stills Still images, relative to the run directory timeline Per-run summary, below complete, error true and null when the run finished; otherwise the error message frame_count, frames Number of frames and one record per frame

Run metadata is a RunInfo:

Field Default Meaning scenario_name Display name of the scenario scenario_id Scenario slug suite conformance Suite the scenario belongs to fps 30 Frames per second duration_s 0.0 Scenario duration in seconds engine ue4 ue4 or ue5 server_version, client_version CARLA versions of the server and the Python client map CARLA map name crosswalk_id Entry of crosswalks.json the scenario was placed on weather clear_noon Weather preset quality standard Quality preset drive Drive mode; the CLI default is kinematic ambient none Ambient traffic level seed 0 Random seed views List of rendered views site Geometry of the site: how the scenario frame maps to the world pipeline_config default Key of decision_testbench.PIPELINE_CONFIGS used for the decision state extra Further options, for example cyclist_proxy (null or "walker")

Each frame record has these keys:

Key Meaning index Frame number, from 0 t Scenario time in seconds, rounded to four decimals state Decision state of the configured pipeline: idle, safe, warning or alert states Decision state per pipeline variant, keyed by name alert_pair [bike_id, ped_id] of the pair that raised the alert, or null danger Ground-truth danger assessment, see Ground truth agents List of agent states, see Ground truth

Images and auxiliary buffers (depth, instance ids) are kept in memory during the run and are not written to the manifest.

The timeline summary is computed from the frame records when the run closes:

Key Meaning frames Number of frames state_counts Frames per decision state alert_intervals, warning_intervals Time intervals in which the pipeline was in that state danger_intervals, actionable_intervals Time intervals labelled dangerous, and those in which a warning is still actionable first_alert_t, first_danger_t Time of the first alert and of the first dangerous frame lead_time_s first_danger_t - first_alert_t closest_approach Frame, time, bike and person ids and distance in metres of the closest bike-pedestrian pair 
import json

manifest = json.load(open("renders/ue4_fast-approach_clear_noon/manifest.json"))

docs.title: Return value of the recorder
docs.text: Code that drives Recorder directly gets the same information from close(): a dictionary with run_dir, manifest, videos, stills and the number of frames written.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problems that come up when starting a CARLA server, connecting to it or rendering a scenario, with the message the tools print and what to do about it. For anything on the client side, start with python -m bikeped.sim probe.

docs.title: Launcher not found
docs.text:
CarlaUnreal.sh not found in /data/carla or /data/carla/Linux. Point --root or CARLA_UE5_ROOT at the folder of the extracted CARLA release.

--root was given and the launcher is in neither place. Without --root the message reads No CARLA ue5 install found and lists every path that was tried: the environment variable first, then the common install paths. The launcher is CarlaUE4.sh for --engine ue4 and CarlaUnreal.sh for --engine ue5, so a UE5 folder passed with --engine ue4 fails the same way.

docs.title: Port already in use
docs.text:
port 2000 on 127.0.0.1 is already in use; stop the server that listens there or choose another --port

Another server, often one left from an earlier session, is listening. Stop it, or start the new one elsewhere and pass the same port to probe and render. A server uses the RPC port and the two ports after it, so keep two servers at least three ports apart.

python -m bikeped.sim server --engine ue5 --port 2010
python -m bikeped.sim probe --port 2010

docs.title: Server exits during start-up
docs.text:
the CARLA server exited with code 1 before it accepted connections; its output is in /tmp/carla_ue4_2000.log

The message is followed by the last 20 lines of the server's output. The full log is in the file it names, carla_<engine>_<port>.log in the system temporary folder.

docs.title: No answer from the server
docs.text:
no answer from the CARLA server on 127.0.0.1:2000 after 180 s

The process is alive and no client could read its version within the timeout. The message includes the last client error and the path of the log file.

docs.title: Missing carla module
docs.text:
The Python client is not installed in the environment that runs the command. Install the wheel that matches the server release:

UE4UE5 
pip install carla==0.9.16

pip install "$CARLA_UE5_ROOT/PythonAPI/carla/dist/carla-0.10.0-cp310-cp310-linux_x86_64.whl"

The 0.10.0 wheel is cp310 only. In an environment with a newer Python, pip rejects it as not supported on the platform. Create a Python 3.10 environment for UE5 work.

docs.title: Client and server version mismatch
docs.text: The client wheel and the server have to come from the same CARLA release. The probe prints both versions, and each manifest stores them as client_version and server_version. Install the wheel of the server's release.

docs.title: Server unreachable
docs.text:
no CARLA server at 127.0.0.1:2000: ...

render and probe connect to --host and --port (default 127.0.0.1:2000). Start a server first, or pass --launch to render so it starts a managed server for the run and stops it afterwards.

docs.title: Engine mismatch
docs.text:
--engine ue5 requested but the server is ue4

--engine on render states which engine you expect; the default auto accepts whatever the server runs. Connect to the other server or drop the flag.

docs.title: No rideable two-wheeler
docs.text:
ue5 server 0.10.0 has no rideable two-wheeler blueprint, so cyclists cannot be rendered. Pass --cyclist-proxy walker to render them as walkers.

The server has no rideable two-wheeler, which is the case for CARLA 0.10.0. Pass --cyclist-proxy walker, or render the scenario on a UE4 server. See UE5 current limits.

docs.title: Sensor timeout
docs.text:
sensor 'fisheye/front' delivered nothing for frame ... within ... s; the server may be overloaded (try --quality draft or fewer views)

Each fisheye view runs one camera per cube face, so a run with several views can exceed what the GPU renders within the timeout. Lower --quality, render fewer views per run, or close other GPU work.

docs.title: Crosswalks on other maps
docs.text: crosswalks.json describes Town10HD_Opt. On another map the renderer reads crosswalk polygons from the live map, and --crosswalk indexes those instead; use --crosswalks-file for a file extracted with tools/carla_find_crosswalks.py (Environment). The probe lists the maps the server can load.

docs.title: Unexpected blueprint
docs.text: The server lacks the preferred blueprint for that model and the renderer used the next one on its list, as described in Actors. Wheelchair walkers exist from CARLA 0.9.16; before that a wheelchair agent is an adult walker. The blueprint field of each agent in manifest.json names what was spawned.

docs.title: CARLA on Unreal Engine 4
docs.text: This page sets up a CARLA 0.9.14, 0.9.15 or 0.9.16 server and its Python client for bikeped.sim and runs a first render. The UE4 line carries the full catalogue of two-wheelers and walkers, so it is the one to use when the agent models matter.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: Item Value CARLA release 0.9.14, 0.9.15 or 0.9.16 Launcher script CarlaUE4.sh, at the top of the extracted release Python client carla wheel of the same release as the server, available for Python 3.10 to 3.12 Install root variable CARLA_UE4_ROOT Maps Town01 to Town15, with Town10HD_Opt as the default here

docs.title: Install the client
docs.text:
The client wheel has to come from the same CARLA release as the server.

pip install carla==0.9.16

bikeped.sim imports carla only when a command talks to a server, so the package imports, and its tests run, on a machine without the wheel.

docs.title: Start the server
docs.text:
export CARLA_UE4_ROOT=/path/to/CARLA_0.9.16
python -m bikeped.sim server --engine ue4
Flag Default Meaning --root PATH $CARLA_UE4_ROOT Folder of the extracted CARLA release --port 2000 RPC port. The server also uses the two ports after it for streaming --quality Epic Epic or Low, passed to the launcher as -quality-level= --windowed off Open a window. Without it the server renders off screen

With --root the command looks only there. Without it, it tries CARLA_UE4_ROOT and then a short list of common install paths. It refuses to start when something already listens on the port, runs the launcher in its own process group, and waits until a client can read the server version. The server's output is written to carla_ue4_<port>.log in the system temporary folder.

The launcher call it builds is equivalent to:

cd "$CARLA_UE4_ROOT"
./CarlaUE4.sh -RenderOffScreen -carla-rpc-port=2000 -quality-level=Epic

docs.title: Probe the server
docs.text:
python -m bikeped.sim probe --host 127.0.0.1 --port 2000

The probe connects, reads the client and server versions, and reports the engine generation, the maps the server can load and the capabilities the renderer depends on. Run it once after installing: a version mismatch or a missing map shows up here, before a render starts.

docs.title: First render
docs.text:
python -m bikeped.sim render --scenario fast-approach --engine ue4 \
    --rig pole,fisheye --weather clear_noon

The run directory is renders/ue4_fast-approach_clear_noon/. Its contents are described in Run output.

docs.title: Notes for this line
docs.text:
Wheelchair walkers exist on 0.9.16, so that is the release to use for the accessibility scenarios. The probe reports whether the connected server has them. See Actors for how scenario models map to blueprints.

crosswalks.json holds the 16 crosswalks of Town10HD_Opt. To render on another town, extract its crosswalks first with tools/carla_find_crosswalks.py, as described in Environment.

carla_scenario.py in the repository root still accepts the options of the single-file runner it replaced and forwards them to python -m bikeped.sim render.

docs.title: CARLA on Unreal Engine 5
docs.text:
This page sets up a CARLA 0.10.0 server and its Python client for bikeped.sim, and lists what to check before a first render. The UE5 line renders with Lumen and Nanite and ships a smaller set of maps and vehicles than UE4.

Validation status

The renderer is developed and run end to end against CARLA 0.9.16 on Unreal Engine 4. The Unreal Engine 5 path follows the CARLA 0.10.0 Python API and is covered by tests against an in-memory stand-in for that API; it has not yet been run against a real CARLA 0.10.0 server. See Current limits.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: Item Value CARLA release 0.10.0 Launcher script CarlaUnreal.sh, in the Linux/ folder of the extracted release Python client carla-0.10.0-cp310-cp310-linux_x86_64.whl, shipped in the release under PythonAPI/carla/dist/ Python version 3.10, the only version the wheel supports Install root variable CARLA_UE5_ROOT Maps Town10HD_Opt and Mine_01

docs.title: Install the client
docs.text:
The 0.10.0 wheel is built for CPython 3.10 only. The rest of the repository runs on Python 3.10 or newer, so one 3.10 environment covers the testbench and both renderers.

export CARLA_UE5_ROOT=/path/to/Carla-0.10.0-Linux-Shipping

python3.10 -m venv .venv-ue5
source .venv-ue5/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install "$CARLA_UE5_ROOT/PythonAPI/carla/dist/carla-0.10.0-cp310-cp310-linux_x86_64.whl"

docs.title: Start the server
docs.text:
python -m bikeped.sim server --engine ue5
Flag Default Meaning --root PATH $CARLA_UE5_ROOT Folder of the extracted CARLA release --port 2000 RPC port. The server also uses the two ports after it for streaming --quality Epic Accepted and ignored: the UE5 launcher has no quality flag --windowed off Open a window. Without it the server renders off screen

The launcher is looked up at the top of the root folder and under Linux/, where the 0.10.0 archive keeps it, so CARLA_UE5_ROOT can point at either. As on UE4, the command refuses to start when the port is taken, waits until a client can read the server version, and writes the server's output to carla_ue5_<port>.log in the system temporary folder.

The launcher call it builds is equivalent to:

cd "$CARLA_UE5_ROOT/Linux"
./CarlaUnreal.sh -RenderOffScreen -carla-rpc-port=2000

docs.title: Probe before rendering
docs.text:
python -m bikeped.sim probe

The probe reads the server's blueprint library at connect time and prints the engine, the versions, the maps and the capabilities the actor code depends on, including whether a rideable two-wheeler exists. On a CARLA 0.10.0 server that check is what decides whether scenarios with cyclists can render at all (see below). Actors describes how scenario models map to blueprints.

docs.title: Current limits
docs.text:
CARLA 0.10.0 ships no rideable bicycle or motorcycle blueprint: its catalogue is four-wheeled vehicles plus walkers. On UE5, render therefore refuses a scenario that contains cyclists unless you pass --cyclist-proxy walker. With that flag a walker stands in for each cyclist, moving along the cyclist's scripted path, and the manifest records the substitution, so a dataset built from the run can tell proxies from real two-wheelers. Pedestrian-only scenarios render as on UE4.

The decision state and the danger label do not change under the proxy, because both read the scripted positions rather than the simulated actor.

docs.title: First render
docs.text:
python -m bikeped.sim render --scenario fast-approach --engine ue5 --rig pole,fisheye --cyclist-proxy walker

The run directory is renders/ue5_fast-approach_clear_noon/. The engine is part of the run id, so UE4 and UE5 renders of the same scenario sit next to each other and can be compared view by view.

docs.title: Notes for this line
docs.text:
The default map and crosswalk carry over: Town10HD_Opt exists on both lines and crosswalks.json was extracted from it. Mine_01 has no entry in crosswalks.json.

The fisheye view renders one camera per cube face where a pinhole view renders one camera in total. Use --quality draft while checking a setup and switch to standard or cinematic for the final pass. See Cameras.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text: bikeped is a collision warning system for crossings shared by pedestrians and cyclists. This page says what the project is, what the repository holds, and where each topic is documented.

docs.title: What the project is
docs.text:
A level fisheye camera on a pole faces across one crosswalk. A Jetson Orin next to it runs an object detector, a ground-plane tracker and a three-stage decision pipeline at 30 FPS, and drives a warning light. Each frame ends in one of four states: idle when no pedestrian is present, safe when a pedestrian is present and no cyclist has been seen in the last 58 frames (about 2 s), warning when both are present, and alert when a cyclist and a pedestrian are closing on each other.

The repository is the companion code of the paper A Real-Time Bike-Pedestrian Safety System with Wide-Angle Perception and Evaluation Testbed for Urban Intersections. The decision logic in it is the file that runs on the device. Around that file sits an offline testbench that replays 24 scripted conformance scenarios through the same logic and produces every number in the paper, so a change to a threshold can be evaluated on a laptop before it reaches an intersection.

docs.title: What is in the repository
docs.text:
Path Contents decision_pipeline.py The three-stage decision logic, imported by both the deployed bridge and the testbench. decision_testbench.py Offline scenario runner: fisheye camera model, detection failure and localisation error models, ground-truth danger labelling, optimizer, Monte Carlo, latency sweep. bikeped/scenarios/ Scenario library: the 24 conformance scenarios and the suites added next to them. bikeped/sim/ CARLA renderer for Unreal Engine 4 and Unreal Engine 5 builds. simulator/index.html Browser simulator in a single HTML file. sim_visualizer.py Schematic 3D renderer that writes one MP4 per scenario. calibration/ Fisheye intrinsic calibration from checkerboard frames. bridge_starter/ Deployment starter kit: one script with a USER CONFIG block. run_experiments.py Runs every experiment in the paper in sequence. config.yaml, camera_calibration.json Runtime parameters and calibrated intrinsics of the deployed system.

The repository layout page lists every file.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: The testbench, the figure scripts and the calibration tools need Python 3.10 or newer and five packages. This page covers that install, the optional pieces (CARLA client, bridge kit, docs toolchain) and a check that it worked.

docs.title: Core install
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/mkturkcan/bikeped.git
cd bikeped
pip install -r requirements.txt

requirements.txt pins lower bounds only:

Package Minimum Used for numpy 1.24 Camera model, scenario interpolation, Monte Carlo. scipy 1.11 Differential evolution in the optimizer, least-squares bundle adjustment in the calibration tools. matplotlib 3.7 Publication figures and the latency sweep plot. pyyaml 6.0 Reading config.yaml. opencv-python 4.8 Scenario videos from sim_visualizer.py, checkerboard detection and frame capture.

None of this needs a GPU. The testbench simulates the detector with a statistical model, so the scenarios run on a laptop CPU.

Run every script from the repository root. The scripts open config.yaml and camera_calibration.json by relative path, and the testbench falls back to built-in camera defaults with the message No camera_calibration.json found, using defaults when it is started somewhere else.

docs.title: Optional pieces
docs.text:
CARLA on UE4CARLA on UE5Bridge starter kitDocs site

The renderer in bikeped/sim talks to a running CARLA server through the carla Python client. For the Unreal Engine 4 line, CARLA 0.9.14 to 0.9.16, client wheels exist for Python 3.10 to 3.12:

pip install carla==0.9.16

The client version has to match the server. python -m bikeped.sim probe prints both.

CARLA 0.10.0 ships a single client wheel, built for CPython 3.10, inside the server package:

pip install Carla-0.10.0-Linux-Shipping/PythonAPI/carla/dist/carla-0.10.0-cp310-cp310-linux_x86_64.whl

If you want to render on both engines from one environment, create it with Python 3.10. The two client versions cannot be installed side by side, so keep one virtual environment per engine.

The kit in bridge_starter/ has its own requirements file, because it runs a real detector:

cd bridge_starter
pip install -r requirements.txt

This adds ultralytics (the YOLO runtime), huggingface_hub (downloads the detector weights on first run) and paho-mqtt (track publishing). play-sounds for audio cues and TensorRT for engine export are installed separately and are both optional. See the starter kit.

pip install mkdocs-material "mkdocstrings[python]" pymdown-extensions
python tools/build_docs.py --serve

The second command builds this site and serves a live preview.

carla is imported lazily. Every module in the repository imports without it, and only the commands that connect to a server need it.

docs.title: Check the install
docs.text:
$ python decision_testbench.py
Loaded calibration: FOV=197.90 cx=1752.7 cy=1804.5 f=1013.3 R=1750 frame=3500x3500 pad=3840 pitch=0 k1=0 k2=0
Running all scenarios with Default pipeline...

The first line confirms that camera_calibration.json was found and read. A table with one row per scenario follows, and the run ends with the totals over all 24 scenarios:

  TOTAL                        1209  361  107 4427 91.9% 92.5%  8.4%

  Alert fatigue (mean fraction of time in alert): 31.9%

The columns are true positives, false positives, false negatives, true negatives (in frames), sensitivity, specificity and severity-weighted false-negative rate. If your totals match, the install is complete. The quickstart explains the table and why these totals differ from the headline numbers in the paper.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: A tour of the repository in five commands: evaluate the pipeline on the conformance scenarios, compare decision rules, render one scenario, open the browser simulator and call the pipeline from Python. It assumes the core install and a shell in the repository root.

docs.title: Run the conformance scenarios
docs.text:
$ python decision_testbench.py
Loaded calibration: FOV=197.90 cx=1752.7 cy=1804.5 f=1013.3 R=1750 frame=3500x3500 pad=3840 pitch=0 k1=0 k2=0
Running all scenarios with Default pipeline...

========================================================================================================================
  SCENARIO RESULTS -- N=58, d=[1.9,24.8]m, v_min=0.147, k=2
========================================================================================================================
  Scenario                       TP   FP   FN   TN   Sens   Spec  SevFN    Lat WarnBgt RxnAdq Fatigue       Exp
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Safe Crossing                   0    0    0  196  0.0% 100.0%  0.0%    N/A     N/A    N/A   0.0%      safe
  Bike Approaches Ped            86   25   14  101 86.0% 80.2% 26.3%   0.47    3.5s   100%  49.1%     alert
  High-Speed Near Miss           97    0   17   82 85.1% 100.0% 18.0%   0.47    3.3s   100%  49.5%     alert
  Multiple VRUs                 113   29    0  114 100.0% 79.7%  0.0%   0.00    3.9s   100%  55.5%     alert
  ...
  Accelerating E-Bike            40    0    6  123 87.0% 100.0%  8.9%   0.20    3.3s   100%  40.7%     alert
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  TOTAL                        1209  361  107 4427 91.9% 92.5%  8.4%

  Alert fatigue (mean fraction of time in alert): 31.9%

The run takes a few seconds. The header line repeats the parameters in use: a cyclist memory of N=58 frames, a distance window of 1.9 to 24.8 m, a minimum cyclist displacement of 0.147 m and a lookback of k=2 frames. These are the values in the decision block of config.yaml.

Each row is one scenario replayed at 30 FPS. TP, FP, FN and TN count frames: a true positive is a frame where the pipeline says alert and the ground-truth safety model labels the frame dangerous. Sens and Spec are the sensitivity and specificity from those counts, SevFN is the false-negative rate weighted by severity, Fatigue is the fraction of the scenario spent in alert, and Exp is the state the scenario author expects to dominate. The testbench page defines the remaining columns.

docs.title: Compare decision rules
docs.text:
--compare runs the same 24 scenarios under each named configuration and adds the fisheye localisation error that the plain run leaves out.

python decision_testbench.py --compare

It prints one table like the one above per configuration. The totals of that run:

Configuration Sensitivity Specificity SevFN Time in alert default 93.3% 92.3% 7.6% 32.3% optimized 93.3% 92.3% 7.6% 32.3% speed_adaptive 93.1% 91.8% 9.4% 33.7% conservative 77.1% 92.6% 31.0% 28.9% proximity_only 56.1% 97.4% 61.5% 19.6% baseline_naive_closing 93.4% 90.4% 7.5% 33.8% baseline_ttc 84.3% 96.4% 14.7% 27.0% baseline_distance_only 57.8% 70.2% 58.5% 41.1%

The default row is the headline result of the paper: 93.3% sensitivity and 92.3% specificity with localisation error. The plain run above reports 91.9% and 92.5% because it evaluates exact positions. python decision_testbench.py --no-bbox-noise --compare reproduces that ablation for every configuration. The three baseline_* rows swap the stage 3 rule for a simpler one, described under decision rules.

docs.title: Render a scenario
docs.text:
sim_visualizer.py draws what the fisheye camera would see: agents projected through the lens model onto a ground-plane wireframe, with the decision state overlaid. Scenario indices are zero-based, so 7 is Fast Approach.

$ python sim_visualizer.py --no-display --scenarios 7
Rendering 1 scenarios, single-cam

  Rendering: Fast Approach (1-cam, 6.5s)
    Saved: sim_07_fast_approach.mp4 (196 frames)

Done.

The MP4 is written to the current directory. Without --no-display the frames also appear in a window while they render.

docs.title: Open the browser simulator
docs.text: The browser simulator runs the same decision logic in a web page. Open simulator/index.html from a checkout, pick a scenario and a pipeline variant, and watch the state change as the agents move. Nothing needs to be installed.

docs.title: Call the pipeline from Python
docs.text:
DecisionPipeline is a plain class with no dependencies beyond the standard library. Feed it one position per tracked object per frame, in ground-plane metres relative to the camera, then ask for the state.

example.py
from decision_pipeline import DecisionPipeline

pipeline = DecisionPipeline(bike_memory_frames=58, prox_min=1.9, prox_max=24.8,
                            prox_speed_min=0.147, lookback_frames=2)

fps = 30
for frame in range(91):
    t = frame / fps
    ped = {'track_id': 1, 'x': 5.0, 'y': -3.0 + 1.4 * t}      # walking across the road
    bike = {'track_id': 2, 'x': 23.0 - 6.0 * t, 'y': 0.5}      # riding toward the crosswalk
    pipeline.update_track(1, ped['x'], ped['y'], t)
    pipeline.update_track(2, bike['x'], bike['y'], t)
    state, pair = pipeline.evaluate([ped], [bike], bike_in_scene=True, sim_time=t)
    if frame % 15 == 0:
        print(f"t={t:4.1f}s  bike x={bike['x']:5.1f} m  state={state:7s}  pair={pair}")

$ python example.py
t= 0.0s  bike x= 23.0 m  state=warning  pair=None
t= 0.5s  bike x= 20.0 m  state=alert    pair=(2, 1)
t= 1.0s  bike x= 17.0 m  state=alert    pair=(2, 1)
t= 1.5s  bike x= 14.0 m  state=alert    pair=(2, 1)
t= 2.0s  bike x= 11.0 m  state=alert    pair=(2, 1)
t= 2.5s  bike x=  8.0 m  state=alert    pair=(2, 1)
t= 3.0s  bike x=  5.0 m  state=warning  pair=None

The first frame is a warning because the closing check needs two positions per track. From the second frame on, the pair distance shrinks and the cyclist moves more than prox_speed_min per lookback, so the state is alert and pair names the cyclist and pedestrian track ids. In the last line the two are 0.7 m apart, closer than prox_min, and that pair is skipped. The floor exists so that a rider detected as a separate person does not pair with their own bike.

The constructor defaults are older values than the selected parameters, so pass the decision block of config.yaml explicitly as above. With an empty pedestrian list evaluate returns ('idle', None), and with a pedestrian and no cyclist in memory it returns ('safe', None).

docs.title: Sources of truth
docs.text:
Every number in the paper comes from four files: decision_pipeline.py (the decision logic), decision_testbench.py (scenarios, sensing model and metrics), config.yaml and camera_calibration.json. The rest of the repository imports from them. If you change one of the four, the paper's tables no longer reproduce.

bridge_starter/decision_pipeline.py is identical to the top-level decision_pipeline.py (cmp bridge_starter/decision_pipeline.py decision_pipeline.py prints nothing), kept so that the starter kit can be copied out of the repository on its own. Edit the top-level file and copy it over.

The calibration scripts live only in calibration/ and the utilities only in tools/, so run them with their directory: python calibration/calibrate_fisheye.py, python tools/latency_report.py.

docs.title: Files that scripts write
docs.text:
Scripts read and write these files by relative path, so run them from the repository root. The files that one step writes and a later step reads are:

File Written by Read by camera_calibration.json calibration/calibrate_fisheye.py testbench, visualiser, bridge eval_cache.json tools/eval_models.py decision_testbench.py --eval-cache, generate_figures.py height_pitch_sweep.json run_height_pitch_sweep.py generate_figures.py latency_data.npy the bridge with latency profiling on tools/latency_report.py

docs.title: How the system works
docs.text:
bikeped watches one crosswalk through a pole-mounted fisheye camera and sets a warning light from the ground positions of the pedestrians and cyclists it sees. This page follows one frame from the sensor to the light and names the page that covers each step.

One frame from the fisheye camera through the processing stages to the warning light and MQTT 197.9° fisheye 3.66 m pole Jetson Orin every frame, 30 FPS Crop pad 3840 crop 3500 Detect YOLO at 1280 px Locate pixel to ground x, y Track ids and history Decide three stages Light one colour per state MQTT track messages The live path. Every stage runs once per frame on the edge device.

docs.title: One frame, step by step
docs.text:
Step What happens Where it is configured Capture The camera delivers a 3840 × 2160 frame holding a fisheye image circle that is taller than the sensor. video in config.yaml Crop The frame is padded to 3840 × 3840 and centre-cropped to 3500 × 3500, which puts the 1750 px image circle in the middle of a square frame. preprocessing.pad_size, preprocessing.crop_size Detect A YOLO detector runs on the square frame at 1280 px input size. In the bridge, a person box that overlaps a bike box is relabelled as the rider. detection in config.yaml, RIDER_* in bridge.py Locate The bottom-centre pixel of each box is sent back through the lens model onto the ground plane, giving (x, y) in metres relative to the camera. The bridge precomputes this as a lookup table at start-up. camera in config.yaml, camera_calibration.json Track A ground-plane tracker matches detections to tracks by metric distance and carries a track through missed detections with constant-velocity prediction. GroundPlaneTracker Decide DecisionPipeline evaluates three stages and returns one of four states. decision in config.yaml Act The state sets the light colour, optionally plays a sound, and the tracks are published over MQTT. feedback, mqtt in config.yaml

The geometry of the Locate step is on the perception page and the Decide step on the decision pipeline page.

docs.title: The four states
docs.text:
State Condition Light Sound in the bridge idle No pedestrian is tracked. Blue safe A pedestrian is present and no cyclist has been seen within the memory window. Green Safe cue, if configured warning A pedestrian and a recent cyclist are present, and no pair is closing. Orange alert A cyclist is closing on a pedestrian inside the distance band. Red Alert cue, if configured

The colour mapping is apply_feedback in bridge_starter/bridge.py. The starter kit ships a SimulatedLight that prints each colour change, so the whole path runs without indicator hardware. sim_visualizer.py draws the states in the same four colours.

docs.title: Live and offline paths share the decision code
docs.text:
decision_pipeline.py has no dependency beyond the standard library and is imported unchanged by the bridge and by decision_testbench.py. The testbench replaces the first three steps with scripted agent paths and then puts back the imperfections of a real detector: it projects each agent's 3D box through the same fisheye model to get the bounding-box localisation error, drops detections according to measured recall, and runs the same kind of ground-plane tracker before calling the pipeline. Ground truth for each frame comes from a kinematic safety model that is independent of the pipeline.

That arrangement is why a parameter change in config.yaml can be evaluated on the 24 conformance scenarios before it reaches an intersection. See the testbench for how to run it.

docs.title: In this section
docs.text:

    The fisheye lens model, the sensor crop, ground-plane back-projection and the bounding-box error.

  • Decision pipeline

    The three stages as coded, every parameter, and the baseline decision rules.

  • Safety model

    Braking profiles, pedestrian reaction time and how a frame is labelled dangerous.

  • Detection and localisation uncertainty

    Missed-detection models, position uncertainty and the tracker used offline.

docs.title: Decision pipeline
docs.text:
The decision logic is one class, DecisionPipeline in decision_pipeline.py, imported by both the live bridge and the offline testbench. This page describes the three stages as they are coded, every parameter with its unit, and the alternative Stage 3 rules that the paper uses as baselines.

The three decision stages and the four states they can return Tracks persons, bikes ground x, y (m) Stage 1 Pedestrian present? any person track Stage 2 Cyclist in memory? seen in the last N frames Stage 3 Pair close and closing? d_min ≤ d ≤ d_max, d falling, cyclist moving yes yes no no no yes idle safe warning alert light: blue light: green light: orange light: red evaluated once per frame Each frame passes through the stages in order and leaves at the first one that fails.

docs.title: Inputs and outputs
docs.text:
The pipeline works on ground-plane positions in metres, relative to the camera. Per frame the caller records every tracked object with update_track(track_id, x, y, t) and then calls evaluate(persons, bikes, bike_in_scene, sim_time), where persons and bikes are lists of {'track_id', 'x', 'y'} dicts. The return value is (state, alert_pair): the state is one of idle, safe, warning, alert, and alert_pair is (bike_track_id, ped_track_id) for an alert and None otherwise.

The object keeps two pieces of state between frames: the cyclist memory buffer and a history of the last 60 positions per track. Call reset() between scenarios when you run it offline.

from decision_pipeline import DecisionPipeline

pipe = DecisionPipeline(bike_memory_frames=58, prox_min=1.9, prox_max=24.8,
                        prox_speed_min=0.147, lookback_frames=2)

ped = {'track_id': 1, 'x': 0.0, 'y': 8.0}
print(pipe.evaluate([], [], bike_in_scene=False, sim_time=0.0))
print(pipe.evaluate([ped], [], bike_in_scene=False, sim_time=0.0))

# A cyclist rides toward the standing pedestrian at 6 m/s.
for frame in range(4):
    t = frame / 30
    bike = {'track_id': 2, 'x': 12.0 - 6.0 * t, 'y': 8.0}
    pipe.update_track(1, ped['x'], ped['y'], t)
    pipe.update_track(2, bike['x'], bike['y'], t)
    state, pair = pipe.evaluate([ped], [bike], bike_in_scene=True, sim_time=t)
    print(f't={t:.3f} s  {state:<7}  pair={pair}')

('idle', None)
('safe', None)
t=0.000 s  warning  pair=None
t=0.033 s  alert    pair=(2, 1)
t=0.067 s  alert    pair=(2, 1)
t=0.100 s  alert    pair=(2, 1)

The first frame with both agents returns warning because Stage 3 needs two history points per track before it can tell whether a pair is closing.

docs.title: Stage 1: pedestrian presence
docs.text: If persons is empty the result is idle. Cyclists alone never raise the state.

docs.title: Stage 2: cyclist memory
docs.text:
Every frame with bike_in_scene=True appends sim_time to a buffer, and entries older than bike_memory_frames / fps seconds are dropped. If the buffer is empty the result is safe. The memory keeps the system out of safe for about two seconds (58 frames at 30 FPS) after a cyclist was last detected, which covers missed detections and short occlusions.

Setting bike_memory_frames to 0 turns the memory off. Stage 2 then looks only at the bikes list of the current frame.

docs.title: Stage 3: pairwise closing check
docs.text:
For every bike and every pedestrian that are both within max_range of the camera:

  1. The current distance d_cur between them must lie in [prox_min, d_max].
  2. Both tracks need at least two history points.
  3. The lookback is min(lookback_frames, len(bike_hist) - 1, len(ped_hist) - 1) frames. d_prev is the distance between the two agents at that earlier frame, using the earlier position of both.
  4. The pair raises alert when d_cur < d_prev and the bike has moved more than prox_speed_min metres over the lookback.

The first pair that passes ends the evaluation. If no pair passes, the result is warning: a pedestrian and a recent cyclist are both present and no pair passes the closing check.

prox_speed_min is a displacement over the lookback window. With the deployed values, 0.147 m over 2 frames at 30 FPS is about 2.2 m/s, so a cyclist who is stopped or walking the bike does not trigger an alert.

docs.title: Speed-adaptive upper bound
docs.text:
With speed_adaptive=True the upper distance bound grows with cyclist speed:

d_max  = max(prox_max, d_stop)
d_stop = v * cyclist_reaction_s + v^2 / (2 * cyclist_decel_ms2)

v is estimated from the track history over the last four intervals. With the default braking values (0.84 s, 1.96 m/s²) stopping_distance returns 14.22 m at 6 m/s, 23.05 m at 8 m/s and 33.91 m at 10 m/s, so against the deployed prox_max of 24.8 m the bound only expands for cyclists faster than 8 m/s. max_range still applies: agents farther than 25 m from the camera are skipped whatever d_max is. The braking values come from the safety model.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Constructor default Deployed (config.yaml) Unit Meaning bike_memory_frames 77 58 frames Length of the cyclist memory. 0 disables it. prox_min 0.5 1.9 m Lower bound on bike to pedestrian distance. Rejects a rider's own body detected as a person. prox_max 20.7 24.8 m Upper bound on bike to pedestrian distance before speed adaptation. prox_speed_min 0.098 0.147 m per lookback Minimum bike displacement over the lookback window. lookback_frames 1 2 frames How far back the closing comparison looks. max_range 25.0 25 m Agents farther than this from the camera are ignored. speed_adaptive True true Expand d_max to the stopping distance. cyclist_reaction_s 0.84 0.84 s Cyclist perception-reaction time. cyclist_decel_ms2 1.96 1.96 m/s² Cyclist braking deceleration. fps 30 frames/s Converts bike_memory_frames to seconds. decision_rule 'pairwise' Stage 3 rule, see below. ttc_threshold_s 3.0 s Threshold for the ttc rule only.

The deployed column is the decision: block of config.yaml, and the same values are the default entry of PIPELINE_CONFIGS in the testbench and the DEC_* constants of the bridge starter kit. config.yaml and the testbench's DecisionParams also carry max_object_age (10 frames), which make_pipeline does not pass to DecisionPipeline.

docs.title: Stage 3 rules
docs.text:
decision_rule swaps the test applied to a pair that is inside the distance band. Stages 1 and 2 are the same for all four.

Rule Alerts when pairwise d_cur < d_prev, with d_prev computed from the earlier positions of both agents, and the bike displacement exceeds prox_speed_min. distance_only The pair is inside [prox_min, d_max]. The rule does not use track history. naive_closing d_cur is smaller than the distance from the bike's earlier position to the pedestrian's current position, and the bike displacement exceeds prox_speed_min. ttc The closing speed (d_prev - d_cur) / dt is above 0.1 m/s and d_cur / closing speed is below ttc_threshold_s.

docs.title: Named configurations
docs.text:
PIPELINE_CONFIGS in decision_testbench.py holds the eight configurations that --compare runs.

Name N (frames) d_min (m) d_max (m) v_min (m) k (frames) Speed-adaptive Rule default 58 1.9 24.8 0.147 2 yes pairwise conservative 60 1.5 15.0 0.05 3 no pairwise proximity_only 0 2.0 10.0 0.1 3 no pairwise speed_adaptive 60 1.0 20.0 0.05 2 yes pairwise optimized 58 1.9 24.8 0.147 2 yes pairwise baseline_distance_only 58 1.9 10.0 0.0 2 no distance_only baseline_naive_closing 58 1.9 24.8 0.147 2 yes naive_closing baseline_ttc 58 1.9 24.8 0.0 2 yes ttc

The TOTAL rows of that run, one per configuration. Counts are frames at 30 FPS summed over the 24 scenarios, with the fisheye localisation error applied (the default).

Configuration TP FP FN TN Sensitivity Specificity Severity-weighted FN Time in alert default 1228 370 88 4418 93.3% 92.3% 7.6% 32.3% conservative 1015 354 301 4434 77.1% 92.6% 31.0% 28.9% proximity_only 738 125 578 4663 56.1% 97.4% 61.5% 19.6% speed_adaptive 1225 392 91 4396 93.1% 91.8% 9.4% 33.7% optimized 1228 370 88 4418 93.3% 92.3% 7.6% 32.3% baseline_distance_only 761 1429 555 3359 57.8% 70.2% 58.5% 41.1% baseline_naive_closing 1229 460 87 4328 93.4% 90.4% 7.5% 33.8% baseline_ttc 1109 173 207 4615 84.3% 96.4% 14.7% 27.0%

Sensitivity is counted over actionable danger frames and specificity over frames with no danger; both terms are defined in the safety model. The naive closing rule reaches the same sensitivity as the pairwise rule with 90 more false-positive frames, because comparing against the pedestrian's current position reads a pedestrian walking toward the bike's old position as the bike closing. Distance alone alerts on 1429 safe frames.

docs.title: Perception geometry
docs.text:
A detection becomes a ground position by sending the bottom-centre pixel of its bounding box back through the fisheye lens model onto the ground plane. This page covers the lens model, the sensor crop, the back-projection, and the localisation error that the bounding-box shortcut introduces. The code is FisheyeCamera and compute_bbox_error in decision_testbench.py.

Side view of a ray from the camera to the ground, and where that ray lands in the fisheye image side view h optical axis, pitch 0 θ ground point d = h / tan θ 3500 × 3500 crop off sensor off sensor row 670 row 2829 (u, v) r = f θ (cx, cy) on sensor image circle, R = 1750 px Left: for a level camera and a ray in the vertical plane of the optical axis, the ray at angle θ meets the ground at d = h / tan θ. Right: the same ray lands at radius r = f θ from the principal point; only rows 670 to 2829 of the crop are on the sensor.

docs.title: Lens model
docs.text:
The deployed lens follows the equidistant model. The angle θ between a ray and the optical axis maps to an image radius

r = f * theta                               # k1 = k2 = 0
r = f * (theta + k1*theta^3 + k2*theta^5)   # with radial correction

FisheyeCamera derives the focal length from the field of view and the image circle radius, f = 2R * 180 / (fov_deg * pi), which gives 1013.3 px for R = 1750 px and a 197.9° field of view. config.yaml names four projection models; the bridge's fisheye_pixel_to_ground handles all of them, and the testbench implements the equidistant one with the optional k1, k2 terms.

camera.projection Model Formula linear equidistant r = f * theta equalarea equisolid r = 2f * sin(theta/2) stereographic stereographic r = 2f * tan(theta/2) orthographic orthographic r = f * sin(theta)

The intrinsics come from camera_calibration.json, written by the calibration tools:

Key Value Unit cx, cy 1752.69, 1804.54 px in the 3500 × 3500 crop focal_length 1013.31 px per radian fov_deg 197.9 degrees radius_px 1750.0 px k1, k2 0.0, 0.0 rms_error_px 4.6334 px, over 1470 points in 42 frames

docs.title: Sensor crop
docs.text: The lens draws a 3500 px image circle, and the sensor is 3840 × 2160, so the top and bottom of the circle fall off the sensor. Preprocessing pads the frame to 3840 × 3840 and centre-crops 3500 × 3500. In that crop the sensor covers rows 670 to 2829 and every column. pixel_on_sensor encodes this band, and a projected point counts as visible only if it is inside the field of view and inside the band.

docs.title: Camera pose in the testbench
docs.text:
Field Value Meaning cam_x, cam_y 5.0, −13.0 Position in the scenario frame, in metres. The crosswalk centre is at (5, 0). height 3.6576 Metres, read from camera.height (12 feet). heading_deg 90 Chosen automatically: 90° when cam_y < 0, 270° otherwise. pitch_deg 0 Level optical axis, read from camera.pitch_deg. Negative values tilt down.

The camera frame is x right, y down, z along the optical axis. All positions handed to the decision pipeline are relative to the camera.

docs.title: Forward and inverse projection
docs.text:
world_to_pixel rotates a world point into the camera frame, takes theta = arccos(z / |d|) and phi = atan2(y, x), applies the lens model and returns u = cx + r cos(phi), v = cy + r sin(phi). A point is valid when theta is below half the field of view and it lies in front of the camera plane.

pixel_to_ground inverts this. It converts the pixel radius to theta (in closed form, or with six Newton iterations when k1 or k2 is non-zero), builds the camera-frame ray (sin θ cos φ, sin θ sin φ, cos θ), rotates it into the world frame and intersects it with the plane z = 0. Rays that do not point downward return NaN and valid = False.

docs.title: Bounding-box localisation error
docs.text:
A detector returns a box, and the system takes the bottom-centre of that box as the point where the object touches the ground. Under fisheye distortion that pixel is not the projection of the true ground point. compute_bbox_error measures the difference:

  1. Build the eight corners of the object's 3D box at ground position (gx, gy) with a given heading (object_3d_corners).
  2. Project the corners and keep the ones on the sensor.
  3. Take the tightest axis-aligned box around them and its bottom-centre pixel.
  4. Back-project that pixel to the ground. The error is the distance between this estimate and (gx, gy).

The object sizes are in OBJECT_TYPES:

Type Length (m) Width (m) Height (m) COCO class AP AR pedestrian 0.3 0.5 1.7 0 0.678 0.755 cyclist 1.8 0.6 1.7 1 0.634 0.740 car 4.5 1.8 1.5 2 0.550 0.629 motorcycle 2.2 0.8 1.4 3 0.680 0.754 bus 12.0 2.5 3.0 5 0.820 0.860 truck 7.0 2.5 2.8 7 0.746 0.806

--error-map prints the error at fixed distances and bearings from the camera for the pedestrian, cyclist and car types:

$ python decision_testbench.py --error-map
Camera: pos=(5.0,-13.0), h=3.6576m, heading=90.0deg, pitch=0.0deg, FOV=197.9deg, R=1750px
...
  PEDESTRIAN (0.3m x 0.5m x 1.7m)
  Heading = 0deg from camera axis
  Dist (m)   Angle       gx       gy   Err (m)   Rel Err      BBox WxH  Corners
       3.0      0deg     5.00   -10.00    0.2479     8.26%        96x389        8
       3.0     80deg     2.05   -12.48    2.1337    71.12%       162x128        4
      10.0      0deg     5.00    -3.00    0.2493     2.49%        31x172        8
      10.0     80deg    -4.85   -11.26    0.3449     3.45%       108x242        8
      25.0      0deg     5.00    12.00    0.2497     1.00%         12x70        8
...
  CYCLIST (1.8m x 0.6m x 1.7m)
  Heading = 0deg from camera axis
      10.0      0deg     5.00    -3.00    0.2730     2.73%       185x175        8
      10.0     30deg     0.00    -4.34    0.5676     5.68%       199x199        8
      20.0     30deg    -5.00     4.32    0.5832     2.92%         98x97        8

Straight ahead of the camera a pedestrian is misplaced by about 0.25 m at every distance from 3 m to 25 m, so the relative error falls from 8.26% to 1.00%. The error grows toward the edge of the field of view, and it jumps where the sensor band clips the box: at 3 m and 80° only four of the eight corners are on the sensor and the estimate is 2.13 m off. A cyclist is longer than a pedestrian, so the error depends more on bearing and heading, reaching 0.57 m at 10 m and 30°.

The error is a function of position, heading and object size, with no random part. When the testbench runs with the error model on, which is the default, it replaces each agent's true position with the estimate before tracking. compute_error_grid evaluates the same function on a 0.5 m grid out to 25 m for the error-map figure. The uncertainty page shows how the results change with the model off.

docs.title: Safety model
docs.text: The testbench needs a ground truth for "this frame is dangerous" that does not depend on the decision pipeline. It gets one from a kinematic model built on cyclist braking profiles, a pedestrian reaction time and a conflict zone around the pedestrian. This page lists the constants with the sources cited in the code and states the labelling rule exactly.

docs.title: Cyclist braking profiles
docs.text:
A profile is a perception-reaction time and a braking deceleration (CyclistBrakingProfile). The stopping distance is

d_stop = v * prt_s + v^2 / (2 * decel_ms2)
Key PRT (s) Deceleration (m/s²) Source given in the code bicycle 0.84 1.96 Martin & Bigazzi 2025, 85th percentile, field measurements, n = 302 (doi) ebike 0.84 6.0 PRT as above; deceleration from Naude et al. 2025, mean maximum in track tests, n = 127 (doi) aashto 2.5 3.4 AASHTO, A Policy on Geometric Design of Highways and Streets, 7th ed. (2018)

bicycle is the default. A scenario selects another profile with its vehicle key, and the profile then drives both the ground-truth labels and the speed-adaptive bound of the pipeline under test, because make_pipeline passes the profile's values to DecisionPipeline. The E-Scooter and Accelerating E-Bike conformance scenarios use ebike. The aashto profile is there for reference against design guidance.

Stopping distances returned by stopping_distance for each profile:

Profile 4 m/s 6 m/s 8 m/s 10 m/s bicycle 7.44 m 14.22 m 23.05 m 33.91 m ebike 4.69 m 8.04 m 12.05 m 16.73 m aashto 12.35 m 20.29 m 29.41 m 39.71 m

docs.title: Pedestrian and conflict-zone constants
docs.text: Constant Value Unit Meaning PEDESTRIAN_REACTION_S 1.87 s Reaction time of a distracted pedestrian (Fugger et al. 2000, combined average). PEDESTRIAN_CLEAR_SPEED_MS 1.3 m/s Walking speed to clear the conflict zone. CONFLICT_ZONE_HALF_WIDTH_M 1.0 m Half-width of the zone the pedestrian occupies. SWERVE_FRICTION_MU 0.4 Tyre-road friction assumed for a swerve. MAX_SEVERITY_SPEED_MS 12.0 m/s Cyclist speed at which severity reaches 1. ACTIONABLE_TTC_LOWER 1.87 s Shortest time to collision at which a warning can still help.

docs.title: Swerve time
docs.text:
A cyclist can also avoid the pedestrian by moving sideways out of the conflict zone. The code models that as reaction time plus the time to cover the half-width w under constant lateral acceleration a_lat = mu * g:

a_lat      = 0.4 * 9.81           = 3.92 m/s^2
t_maneuver = sqrt(2 * w / a_lat)  = 0.71 s
t_swerve   = 0.84 + 0.71          = 1.55 s

The result does not depend on forward speed. It is kept as CYCLIST_SWERVE_TIME_S for comparison, and the actionable bound uses the pedestrian's 1.87 s instead: the system exists to warn the pedestrian, so the labels are judged against the pedestrian's response window.

docs.title: Labelling a frame
docs.text:
compute_ground_truth_danger(scenario, t) evaluates every bike and pedestrian pair that is within 25 m of each other at time t and returns one DangerAssessment.

For each pair it computes:

  • the bike speed v from the scripted path and the stopping distance sd under the scenario's braking profile;
  • from time_to_collision, which scans the next 5 s of both paths in 0.05 s steps: the minimum future distance d_min, the time ttc until the distance first drops below the 1.0 m conflict radius, and the current closing speed v_close;
  • the gap to the conflict zone, max(d_cur - 1.0, 0);
  • a time-to-collision threshold, 1.87 s plus the time the pedestrian needs to walk 2.0 m at their current speed. A pedestrian slower than 0.1 m/s cannot clear the zone and gets 30 s.

The pair is dangerous when the paths converge and the cyclist either cannot stop in time or is about to arrive:

is_danger = (
    v_close > 0.3                      # closing, m/s
    and d_min < convergence_m          # 5.0 m: the paths actually converge
    and (sd > gap_to_conflict * stop_margin    # stop_margin = 0.8
         or ttc < ttc_threshold)
)
actionable = is_danger and ttc >= ACTIONABLE_TTC_LOWER
severity   = min((v / MAX_SEVERITY_SPEED_MS) ** 2, 1.0)

The convergence test keeps parallel paths out: two agents can close on each other for a while and still pass more than 5 m apart. Severity scales with the square of cyclist speed, as kinetic energy does.

When several pairs are dangerous the function returns the one with the highest severity. When none is, it returns the pair with the smallest d_min.

docs.title: The DangerAssessment record
docs.text: Field Unit Meaning is_danger The frame is physically threatening. actionable Dangerous, and the time to collision is at least 1.87 s, so a warning can still change the outcome. severity 0 to 1 Squared cyclist speed relative to 12 m/s. ttc s Time until the pair is within 1.0 m; infinite if that does not happen within 5 s. d_min_future m Minimum distance within the 5 s lookahead. closing_speed m/s Positive when the distance is shrinking. bike_speed m/s Cyclist ground speed. stopping_dist m Stopping distance at that speed. warning_budget s Time from this frame to closest approach. distance m Current distance between the pair.

docs.title: How the metrics use the labels
docs.text:
Dangerous frames that are no longer actionable are called imminent in the code. The two tiers are scored differently:

Metric Definition True positive Alert on an actionable frame. False negative No alert on an actionable frame. False positive Alert on a frame with no danger of either tier. True negative No alert on a frame with no danger. Sensitivity True positives over actionable frames. Specificity True negatives over frames with no danger. Severity-weighted FN Summed severity of missed actionable frames over summed severity of all actionable frames. Reaction adequacy Share of alert onsets that leave more than 1.87 s before closest approach.

An alert during an imminent frame counts neither for nor against the system. The alert is correct, and the pedestrian could no longer have used it.
